If someone returns sincerely, even multiple times in the same day, we are called to forgive without reservation. The number seven, in the Bible, is associated with perfection and completeness; to forgive "seven times" is to forgive completely and unconditionally.

sens: The number 7,000
G2035.detail: 1. Seven thousand is simply the number 7,000: neither more nor less. Paul cites a passage from the Old Testament where God tells Elijah that He has reserved seven thousand men in Israel who have not bowed to Baal (Romans 11:4). This number symbolizes a faithful remnant, a minority that God has kept for Himself amidst a majority that is unfaithful.
G2035.origine: The Greek word is composed of two elements: "hepta" (seven) and "chilioi" (thousand). It is a compound number that precisely expresses 7 × 1,000. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, the same passage says "seven thousand." Round numbers like this, especially in God's words, often carry a spiritual significance: they are not always to be interpreted arithmetically, but as symbols of completeness or sufficiency.
G2035.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Romans 11:4. Paul borrows it from the passage in 1 Kings 19:18, where Elijah believes he is the only faithful one to God, but the Lord reveals to him that He has preserved a remnant of seven thousand men who have not bowed their knee to Baal. Paul uses this memory to show that, even in his time, there remains a remnant of Israel chosen by grace, a small number preserved by God among the majority.
G2035.portee: This passage teaches that God never completely abandons His people. Even when everything seems lost or faithfulness appears rare, God always reserves a remnant — a group, perhaps small in number, but genuinely attached to Him. For the believer, this is a source of encouragement: we are never alone, and God counts each of His own, even when we feel isolated in faith.

sens: To express in words, to communicate orally
To respond to someone, to engage in dialogue
To declare, affirm something as true
To command, order
To tell, report a narrative or teaching
G2036.detail:
1. The most basic meaning: to open the mouth and produce words to communicate a thought, information, or feeling. It is the simple act of speaking. Example: in Matthew 5:11, Jesus says, "Blessed are you when they revile you."
2. To respond means that someone speaks in return, often to react to what another has just said. It is to dialogue, to engage in exchange. Example: in Matthew 26:23, facing the disciples, Jesus responds: "He who dipped his hand with me in the dish."
3. To declare or affirm: to express something in a solemn or decisive manner, as a truth. Example: in Matthew 2:5, the scholars say, "In Bethlehem of Judea" in response to the king who asks where the Messiah will be born.
4. To command, order: to say something with the authority of one who must be obeyed. Example: in Acts 5:3, Peter says to Ananias, "Why has Satan filled your heart?" in a manner that carries judgment and authority.
5. To tell or teach: to use words to convey a narrative, a lesson, or a parable. Example: in Luke 18:9, Jesus tells a parable aimed at certain people.
G2036.origine: The word comes from an ancient Greek verb ἔπω (epô) which originally meant "to say" and of which this form eipon is the aorist (the simple past tense in Greek). This aorist tense has become one of the regular forms of the very common verb λέγω (legô), which also means "to say" and is more frequently used in New Testament Greek. The two verbs have merged in usage: eipon and λέγω have become interchangeable to express the action of saying in the past.
G2036.emploi: This verb is one of the most frequent in the New Testament, with about 880 occurrences. It is found everywhere: in Matthew, Mark, Luke, John, and in Acts, as well as in the epistles. It serves to introduce reported speech: "Jesus said" or "He answered." The verb slightly changes nuance depending on the context: it can be a simple statement of fact ("They told him where he was"), a reply that carries emotion or challenge ("You have a demon"), or a command that must be obeyed ("Peter said to him: Ananias..."). In the Gospels, it is the preferred word to report the words of Jesus and the dialogue between characters.
G2036.portee: For the Christian, this verb reminds us of the importance of words in biblical faith. God Himself "said" to create (Genesis), and Jesus "said" to teach, heal, and save. Meditating on what Jesus "said" is a way to encounter His person and authority through the Gospel. It is also an invitation to give weight to our own words: we speak as those who reflect the word of God.

sens: Companion of the apostle Paul in his missionary journeys
Treasurer of the city of Corinth
G2037.detail:
1. Erastus is a collaborator of Paul mentioned in Acts. In Acts 19:22, Paul sends him to Macedonia with Timothy as a missionary aide, while he himself stays in Asia. He is a trusted man of the great apostle, associated with his evangelistic work.
2. The same person (or perhaps a namesake) appears in Romans 16:23 as "the treasurer of the city," meaning the administrator of the municipal finances of Corinth. Paul greets him as a brother in faith. He is an example of a Christian holding a position of civil responsibility.
G2037.origine: The name Erastus comes from Greek and literally means "beloved" or "one who is loved." It is a common name in the Greco-Roman world of the time. It designates here one or two specific personalities from the Pauline circle.
G2037.emploi: Erastus appears three times in the New Testament, always in Pauline contexts. In Acts 19:22, he is an aide of Paul sent on a mission to Macedonia. In Romans 16:23, he is included in the greetings at the end of the epistle and bears the title of treasurer of Corinth. In 2 Timothy 4:20, Paul notes that Erastus "remained in Corinth," which may refer to the same person or a namesake. The three passages do not allow us to conclude with certainty whether it is one or two different individuals.
G2037.portee: Erastus illustrates how the early Church integrated men from all social backgrounds — mission collaborators, civil administrators — into Christian fellowship. His example shows that faith is not limited to the poor or the lowly, but is also rooted in public responsibilities.

sens: To engage in work, a laborious activity to earn a living or accomplish a task
To do, produce, accomplish something, particularly a work, an act, or a practice
To commit, to carry out in the sense of realizing (a good or bad action)
To act, to function (referring to God or a divine power)
G2038.detail:
1. To work means to exert physical or intellectual effort to accomplish a task and live: it is the daily work of the laborer or the artisan. Paul boasts of working with his own hands rather than living at the expense of others (1 Corinthians 4:12), and he reproaches some Thessalonians for not working but meddling in trivialities (2 Thessalonians 3:11).
2. To do or produce a work means to concretely realize something: to accomplish a particular task, to carry out an action. When the master says to the servant, "Go work in my vineyard" (Matthew 21:28), he orders him to perform this specific task. God himself "works a work" among the Gentiles (Acts 13:41).
3. To commit means to realize an action, especially a bad action: these are the reprehensible acts one carries out. Jesus says to those who practice iniquity: "I never knew you; depart from me" (Matthew 7:23). It is also to do good: "Let him who stole steal no longer; but rather let him labor, working with his hands what is good" (Ephesians 4:28).
4. To act or function refers to the action of a divine power: when Jesus states, "My Father has been working until now, and I have been working" (John 5:17), he describes God's continuous activity to sustain the world and fulfill His purpose.
G2038.origine: The word comes from ἔργον (ergon), which means "work" or "labor." It shares the same root found in words like "energy" (in Greek ἐνέργεια, action, force) or "work" in French. In Hebrew, the verb עָבַד (avad) or פָּעַל (paʿal), which mean "to serve" and "to do, to act," are often translated by this term in the Greek Old Testament. The basic image is that of effort, the work produced.
G2038.emploi: The verb appears 39 times in the New Testament, mainly in Paul's epistles. Intransitively (without a complement), it simply means "to work": Paul reports working with his hands (1 Corinthians 4:12, 1 Thessalonians 4:11) and reproves those who live idly (2 Thessalonians 3:11). Transitively (with a complement), it means "to do, to produce, to accomplish": one works good (Romans 2:10, Ephesians 4:28), one commits iniquity or sin (Matthew 7:23, James 2:9), one does a work (John 3:21, Acts 13:41). John often uses the expression "the works of God" to refer to what God accomplishes (John 6:28, 6:30). In Paul, the word also includes the idea of working for a cause or a reward (Romans 4:4-5).
G2038.portee: This word reminds the believer that work is honorable and that idleness is condemned in the Christian life. But it also elevates the perspective: to accomplish a work is to participate in the very activity of God, to bring good, justice, and righteousness into the world. The Christian who works consciously and justly does not merely ensure his livelihood: he cooperates with God to transform the world and serve his neighbor.

sens: professional activity, trade
business or commercial enterprise
profit or gain derived from an activity
execution, realization of an action
G2039.detail:
1. Work refers to the regular activity by which one earns a living: a trade, a profession. Demetrius, the silversmith, makes silver shrines, which constitutes his daily work (Acts 19:24-25).
2. Specifically, it is the business, the commercial enterprise, the source of income: Paul and Silas disturb the work of the masters of the servant by casting out the spirit that possessed her, and these masters therefore lose their source of profit (Acts 16:16, 19).
3. It is also the gain, the financial profit one derives from their work: the masters feared losing their lucrative gain by losing the fortune-teller who enriched them (Acts 16:19).
4. More broadly, it is the execution of an action, the performance: to the Ephesians, Paul speaks of those who "have given themselves over to lewdness to work all uncleanness," where the work of evil means its accomplishment. Luke 12:58 also uses the term to mean "to clear" (to free oneself) from someone, an action to be taken.
G2039.origine: The Greek word comes from the same root as "ergon" (ἔργον, the work, the labor). It is the action noun: if ergon is the work as a result, ergasia is the work, the activity itself. It translates in Greek the Hebrew words "melaka" (work, trade) and "aboda" (labor, service). The word emphasizes less fatigue than the regular exercise of a trade or economic function.
G2039.emploi: The word appears 6 times in the New Testament, concentrated in Acts. It primarily refers to the trade or business one engages in: among the silversmiths of Corinth (Acts 19:24-25) and in the incident with the fortune-teller in Philippi (Acts 16:16, 19). In these contexts, it emphasizes the economic aspect: it is the source of income, the profit derived from an activity. Only once, in Ephesians 4:19, the meaning extends to the execution of any act, here negative ("to commit" evil). In Luke 12:58, the term takes on a nuance of action to be accomplished ("task on the way" = "make the effort").
G2039.portee: This word reminds the believer that daily work, no matter how ordinary, matters to God and fits into His vision. Paul cares about the trades of artisans, about honest profit. He also invites discernment: a job can be a legitimate source of income, but it can also become an instrument of deceit and exploitation (the fortune-teller). The term pushes us to reflect: what work do we do? What is its moral and spiritual profit?

sens: one who works with their hands, especially in the fields
one who practices a trade or work
one who acts, who does something
false apostle or deceptive teacher
G2040.detail:
1. An agricultural worker, a field laborer: Jesus says to his disciples, "The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few" (Matthew 9:37), referring to those who plow and harvest. This is the most concrete meaning of the word.

2. More broadly, any manual worker or artisan who earns a living by their labor: "the laborer is worthy of his food" (Matthew 10:10) or "his wages" (Luke 10:7). The laborer depends on their work for sustenance.

3. One who accomplishes an action, who is the author of a work: in the expression "worker of iniquity" (Luke 13:27), it refers to one who produces, who manufactures evil as an artisan manufactures an object.

4. Specifically, a false teacher or a bad instructor: Paul warns against "evil workers" (Philippians 3:2) who work to deceive Christians, like counterfeiters who produce false goods.
G2040.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb ἐργάζομαι (ergazomai), "to work," itself derived from the root ἔργον (ergon), "work, labor." It literally means "one who does ergon." The word evokes the image of one who puts their energy into work, who produces something through their effort. In the Greek Old Testament, it often translates the Hebrew term that designates the worker or artisan.
G2040.emploi: The word appears 15 times in the New Testament, mainly in Matthew and Luke. In the parables, Jesus uses it to speak of the vineyard workers (Matthew 20) or the spiritual harvest (Matthew 9:37-38, Luke 10:2), where the laborers are lacking and the work awaits. Paul also uses it for the apostles and preachers: they must be "approved workers" (2 Timothy 2:15), meaning recognized as worthy and faithful. But he also uses it ironically or critically to refer to false teachers, the "evil workers" (Philippians 3:2, 2 Corinthians 11:13) who produce lies. The word thus conveys the idea of effort and responsibility.
G2040.portee: This word reminds the Christian that the service of Christ is real work, requiring energy and dedication. It also invites discernment: not everything that presents itself as "spiritual work" is authentic. Finally, it values ordinary work — that of the fields, of the artisan — as worthy of respect and fair wages, freeing the Christian from shame regarding manual labor.

sens: What one does, what one produces with their hands: a job, a task
What one accomplishes, what one realizes: an action, a deed, a gesture
The concrete result of this work: what is produced, created, manufactured
A work of God: the powerful acts of God that reveal His nature and authority
A moral work: a good or bad action in the ethical and spiritual realm
What testifies to living faith: the concrete acts that manifest true belief
G2041.detail:
1. In its simplest sense, the word refers to a job, a task, an employment: what one regularly does with their hands or energy. In Acts 13:2, it refers to the work to which God calls Paul and Barnabas; in John 4:34, Jesus speaks of His food as doing the work of the one who sent Him.
2. More broadly, it is an action, a gesture, a deed that one performs once: what we do that has consequences. Examples abound: in Matthew 23:3, the scribes do not do the works they teach; in John 10:32, Jesus shows several good works coming from His Father.
3. The word can also refer to the object, the result: what is created, produced, manufactured. In Acts 7:41, the Israelites worship a calf forged by their hands. It is the finished product of labor.
4. Very often in John, "work" means a powerful act of God that manifests who He is and what He can do. In John 5:36, Jesus says that the works the Father has given Him to accomplish testify about Him; in Revelation 15:3, they sing of the works of God, great and marvelous.
5. Ethically, a work is a human action judged good or bad before God. In Titus 1:16, those who claim to know God deny Him by their works; in Titus 3:8, Paul wants believers to be diligent in doing good works.
6. The expression "work of faith" or "good work" emphasizes what proves a true relationship with God: acts that stem from conviction and not calculation. In Philippians 1:6, Paul is confident that God will perfect the good work He has begun in them.
G2041.origine: The Greek word ἔργον comes from a very ancient root that evokes effort, action, doing. In biblical Hebrew, it mainly translates מַשֶׂה (masseh, "action, work") and מְלָאכָה (melacha, "work, craft"), as well as עֲבֹדָה (avoda, "service, work"). It is a fundamental word in the Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Old Testament): it appears already in Homer and in classical Greek texts with the same concrete and broad meaning.
G2041.emploi: The word ergon appears about 161 times in the New Testament, especially in Paul (notably in Romans and Galatians where he contrasts the "works of the law" with faith) and in John (where the "works" of Jesus and the Father are at the heart of the testimony). In the Gospel of John in particular, a "work" is often a sign, a powerful act that reveals the identity of the Son or the Father: it is a key term in Johannine Christology. In Paul, the "work" can be either what the Law requires (which does not save by itself) or the concrete act of the Christian that manifests their faith. The word thus covers humble daily action (a task) up to the great act of power (the miracles of Jesus) and ethical judgment (good or bad work).
G2041.portee: This word calls the reader to see that faith is lived out, not just in words. In Matthew 5:16, good works are the believer's light in the world: they glorify the Father. In Paul, he learns to distinguish between false security (saving oneself by one's own efforts) and living obedience: faith without works is dead (James 2). The Bible constantly exhorts to examine one's works and to produce good ones, because the true fruit of a relationship with God is seen in the concrete aspects of life.

sens: Irritate, annoy, provoke anger
Stimulate, encourage to act
G2042.detail:
1. To stir someone to anger or irritation means to provoke them intentionally or unintentionally. This is what fathers do who provoke their children (Colossians 3:21): through their words or behavior, they put them in a state of frustration or discouragement.
2. To stir up in a positive sense means to stimulate someone, encourage them, motivate them to act well. Thus, the zeal of the Corinthians stimulated the Macedonians to engage generously (2 Corinthians 9:2): seeing their enthusiasm, others were encouraged to do the same.
G2042.origine: The word comes from a Greek root that expresses the idea of poking, shaking, disturbing. It has a fundamental concrete sense: to agitate something, and then it has taken on a figurative sense to describe the inner agitation caused by emotions or motivations. The Bible uses it for situations of tension (irritation) or positive momentum (stimulation).
G2042.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament. In Colossians 3:21, it describes a warning to fathers: not to irritate their children. It is a call to parental kindness, not to be harsh. In 2 Corinthians 9:2, Paul uses the same verb but with a positive connotation: the zeal of the Corinthians has stirred up, excited a generous momentum among the Macedonians. The context is that of the collection for the poor in Jerusalem. The word changes meaning depending on its context: destructive irritation on one side, beneficial stimulation on the other.
G2042.portee: This word reminds the reader of two simple but strong lessons. First, parents must cultivate gentleness: parental anger destroys the child, while kindness encourages them. Secondly, our actions can inspire or discourage others. Our commitment to good can be contagious, prompting others to follow our example. It is a call to responsibility: not to harm those entrusted to us, but rather to invigorate them through our zeal and love.

sens: To run a ship aground on land or a reef to block it
To immobilize a boat by grounding it in sand or rocks
G2043.detail:
1. The word refers to the action of intentionally or unintentionally grounding a ship on land, on a sandbank, or a reef, to put it out of danger or to block it. In Acts 27:41, this is exactly what happens: the ship carrying Paul encounters a stretch of land, and the sailors intentionally run the boat aground; the bow sinks into the sand and remains still, allowing the passengers to jump and reach the shore.
2. The word can also express the general idea of firmly immobilizing, fixing something in place by force or support. This is why some older translations render the word as "to sink" or "to block": the image is of an object pressed so hard that it can no longer move.
G2043.origine: The Greek word comes from a root that evokes the idea of pressing against something, pushing it against a surface. It is found in Greek poetry and in later texts. In Hebrew, the Greek translators often used this word to render the verb תָּמַךְ (tamak), which means "to support" or "to press": it is about firmly holding something in place.
G2043.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 27:41, during the shipwreck of the vessel carrying the apostle Paul to Rome. In this detailed account of the storm, the captain and the sailors, seeing a bay with a beach, decide to drive the ship there. The bow runs aground on the sand and sinks, while the stern, remaining in deeper water, is broken by the waves. This is a decisive moment in the journey: the ship is lost, but all the passengers and crew will manage to reach the shore safely, as Paul had promised.
G2043.portee: This word reminds us how God protects His servants in the midst of storms and dangers. The shipwreck itself, which could have been a disaster, becomes the means by which everyone is saved: the firmness of the ship run aground on the sand allows everyone to escape. It is an image of divine help that turns our apparent misfortunes into deliverance.

sens: To pronounce words, to make a speech
To express what was hidden or forgotten
To solemnly proclaim a truth, a message
G2044.detail:
1. The verb primarily evokes the action of speaking aloud, uttering words — a strong and clear vocal expression. The Greek word has as its first image the roaring of a wild animal or the bellowing of an ox, and then it extended to vibrant and sonorous human language: thus in Matthew 13:35, the Father "opens His mouth" to "publish" His words.
2. In the biblical context, "publish" specifically means to express and reveal what has remained secret, invisible, or relegated to forgetfulness. It is a bringing to light, a disclosure: the things "hidden since the foundation of the world" become intelligible and audible.
3. The term also carries the nuance of solemn proclamation, a message that is not kept to oneself but is openly delivered to all. It is the action of the prophet or of one who holds an important word and makes it known publicly.
G2044.origine: The Greek word comes from a root that evokes violent noise: the roar of a wild animal. In the Greek Old Testament, it primarily translates the Hebrew verb שָׁאַג (sa'ag), which means to roar or to growl. From this first image of the powerful noise of the animal, the word has refined to designate energetic and solemn human language — the transition from a raw cry to articulated speech.
G2044.emploi: The verb appears only once in the New Testament: Matthew 13:35, where Jesus quotes Psalm 78:2. The context is that of teaching in parables: by this choice of word, the Bible emphasizes that Jesus does not murmur, does not whisper, but fully proclaims the wisdom and mysteries of the Kingdom. The basic animal image has completely disappeared; what remains is the idea of audible, carried speech that is heard and made known. It is a term suitable for the solemn moment when the eternal secrets of God are brought to light.
G2044.portee: This word reminds the reader of the power and clarity of the evangelical message. Jesus does not teach in a whisper, in secret: He "publishes" the mysteries hidden since the foundation of the world. For the believer, it is the assurance that the Good News is not an obscure murmur, but a strong proclamation meant to be received and heard by all.

sens: to examine carefully, to seek to know in depth
to probe, to scrutinize hidden thoughts or intentions
to actively seek, to investigate
G2045.detail:
1. To search means to examine something carefully to truly know it. Jesus tells His listeners: "You search the Scriptures" (John 5:39), meaning you study them, you go through them in detail to find eternal life. It is an active and meticulous search.
2. The word also denotes an inspection of hidden thoughts or intentions, those that only God can truly perceive. God "searches the hearts" (Romans 8:27): He knows not only what you do, but also what you truly think, your secret motivations. The Holy Spirit "searches all things, even the depths of God" (1 Corinthians 2:10), meaning He accesses the most hidden and mysterious realities.
3. The word can also mean to seek to know, to investigate: the Pharisees ask Nicodemus to "examine" whether a prophet can come from Galilee (John 7:52), meaning to verify what is really the case by consulting the Scriptures.
G2045.origine: The Greek word ἐρευνάω comes from a root that evokes the idea of searching, of probing. It translates several Hebrew verbs in Greek, notably חָקַר (haqar, "to examine, to search") and חָפַשׂ (haphash, "to probe"). These Hebrew verbs retain the concrete image of probing a place or thing to discover what is hidden. It is this image of penetrating search that remains at the heart of the Greek word: accessing what is not visible at first glance.
G2045.emploi: The verb ἐρευνάω is infrequent in the New Testament (6 documented uses). It mainly appears in John and Paul to describe a thorough search or examination. In John, Jesus invites His listeners to search the Scriptures (John 5:39) and the Pharisees to examine the Law (John 7:52) — it is an intellectual quest for knowledge. In Paul and Revelation, the word takes on a more divine and mysterious dimension: God searches the hearts (Romans 8:27, Revelation 2:23), the Spirit searches the depths of God (1 Corinthians 2:10), and the prophets of the Old Testament sought to search the meaning of the revelations they received (1 Peter 1:11). In all cases, it is a serious search, an investigation that goes beyond appearances.
G2045.portee: This word reminds us that knowing God and understanding His word requires true searching, serious meditation on the Scriptures. But it also reminds us that no human search escapes God: He "searches the hearts," He knows not only our actions but also our true motivations. It is a call to inner honesty before God and to humility in our approach to the truth.

sens: To pronounce words, to express a thought through speech
To declare something solemnly or officially
To report what someone else has said
To mean, to signify
To write or record in writing
To call, to designate by a name
G2046.detail:
1. To say is primarily to express a thought by pronouncing words. It is the verb of common speech, used to report what someone has said, whether it be a direct question or a simple statement: Jesus answered, "My grace is sufficient for you" (2 Corinthians 12:9), or the apostle declares, "Pray to the Lord for me" (Acts 8:24).
2. To say can also mean to affirm something solemnly or with authority, to announce a word that commits the one who pronounces it. This applies particularly to prophecies: "All this took place to fulfill what the Lord had spoken by the prophet" (Matthew 1:22). It is a word that does not remain without effect.
3. In some cases, to say reports the words of another, as when introducing a quotation or a previous statement: "It is said: You shall not put the Lord your God to the test" (Luke 4:12). Here, it refers to what has been stated before.
4. To say can also mean to signify or to intend, to express a hidden meaning or intention: the word then carries a deeper meaning than its mere words.
5. To say is also used for writing: when one "says" through Holy Scripture, it amounts to saying what is written, what is recorded in the text.
6. Finally, to say can mean to call or to name, to give someone a name: to designate someone by a certain title or quality.
G2046.origine: The Greek verb λέγω comes from an ancient root that originally meant "to gather, to collect" (hence "to count, to enumerate"), before evolving to the meaning of "to say" or "to speak." This semantic shift reflects the image of one who "gathers" his thoughts and "articulates" them in words. In Hebrew of the Old Testament, λέγω frequently translates אָמַר (amar), the classic verb for saying. There are several compounds in Greek: προλέγω (to say beforehand), διαλέγομαι (to converse), συλλέγω (to gather). The Latin verb dicere has the same distant root.
G2046.emploi: This verb is one of the most frequent in the New Testament, used 49 times among the provided references. It is the verb par excellence of direct and indirect speech. It introduces the words of Jesus, the apostles, the prophets, and God Himself. In Matthew and Mark, it frames the teachings of the Lord and the dialogues with His disciples. In Acts, it reports the speeches of Peter and the apostles. A particular usage in Matthew and Luke: to say that the prophecy is "fulfilled" or that it "is being fulfilled" (Matthew 1:22, Luke 4:12). It can also introduce an unspoken thought (thought of the heart), a written word, or signify a deeper meaning. The verb λαλέω, a synonym, emphasizes more the act of speaking; λέγω emphasizes the content and meaning.
G2046.portee: This simple yet dense word reminds the reader of the power of speech in the Bible. Every time God "says" something, it comes to pass: His word creates and fulfills. For us, hearing what God has "said" in Scripture is to listen to a word that engages our obedience and faith. It is also to learn that the words we pronounce are never neutral: they reveal who we are and carry a responsibility before God.

sens: Wild and uninhabited region, lacking resources
Isolated space far from any habitation
State of solitude or abandonment
G2047.detail: 1. The desert is a wild and barren region, far from civilization and cities. It is a place where it is difficult to find food or help: the disciples ask Jesus how to provide bread for the crowd "in this desolate place" (Matthew 15:33), because resources are lacking there. 2. The word also refers to any isolated and solitary space, far from human dwellings — like the deserts traversed by Paul during his missionary journeys (2 Corinthians 11:26), where he faces a thousand dangers far from any help. 3. It can evoke a state of deep solitude and deprivation: men of faith wandering "in deserts and mountains, in caves and holes in the ground" (Hebrews 11:38) live an existence of exile and abandonment from the world.
G2047.origine: The Greek word comes from the adjective "erēmos" (ἔρημος), which means "empty, solitary, desolate." It is the image of a place emptied of all human presence and life. The Hebrew word it often translates is "haraba" (חָרַב) or "shemama" (שְׁמָמָה), which have the same meaning of desolation and ruin. This family of words everywhere evokes the idea of absence and emptiness.
G2047.emploi: The word appears four times in the New Testament, always to designate a remote and inhospitable physical place. Matthew and Mark use it for the desert where Jesus feeds the crowd: it is a remote place where finding food is impossible. Paul mentions it in his list of perils (2 Corinthians 11:26): traveling in the desert means facing isolation and danger. Hebrews 11:38 uses it to describe the hidden life of the faithful of the Old Testament, who withdrew into extreme solitudes rather than compromise their faith. The desert is always here a refuge or a trial, never just a simple landscape.
G2047.portee: For the Christian, the desert of the New Testament is not just a geography: it is the symbol of trial, isolation, and the renunciation accepted for faith. The heroes of faith in Hebrews 11 show us that the desert — the abandonment of the world, solitude — can be the very place where God manifests His power and faithfulness. This word reminds us that living by faith sometimes exposes one to the hostility of the world and isolation, but that it is not a defeat: it is a possible path, a place where one can meet God away from the illusions of the world.

sens: Arid and sparsely populated region, far from cities and dwellings
Wild place where one is alone and isolated
State of a person or place abandoned, without inhabitants
Territory where God shapes and prepares His people
G2048.detail: 1. The desert is an arid and vast region, far from inhabited areas — it is a natural space where few or no people live. John the Baptist preached in the desert of Judea (Matthew 3:1), far from the cities, to announce the coming of the Messiah. 2. It is a place of solitude where one is left to oneself, facing the wild and often hostile nature. Jesus withdrew there to pray (Luke 5:16) and was tempted by the devil there (Matthew 4:1). 3. The word also applies to what is abandoned, devoid of inhabitants. The temple of Jerusalem, rejected by Jesus, was left desolate (Matthew 23:38). 4. In the history of Israel, the desert is the quintessential place where God educates, tests, and meets His people — forty years of wandering in the desert of Sinai (Acts 7:36-38) form a new generation. It is a spiritual space as much as a geographical one.
G2048.origine: The Greek word erēmos comes from a root denoting absence or isolation. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, it primarily translates "midbar," which also means "pasture" or "place of pasture" — the desert is not always barren; it is primarily a wild space away from habitation. The Greek word retains this dual meaning: geographical isolation and moral solitude.
G2048.emploi: The word erēmos appears about 50 times in the New Testament, especially in the first three Gospels (Matthew, Mark, Luke) and in Acts. It primarily designates the geographical desert of Judea and Sinai: John baptizes there (Mark 1:3-4), Jesus is tempted for forty days (Matthew 4:1), the crowd follows Jesus there (Matthew 14:13). The word is also used to describe a remote and infrequently visited place: Jesus and His disciples withdraw there to rest (Mark 6:31-32). It finally designates the state of abandonment: a woman can be described as "forsaken" (Galatians 4:27), the temple of Jerusalem remains empty and without inhabitants (Matthew 23:38). In the Epistle to the Hebrews, the desert evokes Israel's wandering and the trials of faith (Hebrews 3:8, 3:17).
G2048.portee: The desert in the Bible is not just a landscape: it is the school of faith. Jesus and John the Baptist go there to prepare for their mission and to meet God away from the noise of the world. For the Christian, this teaches that isolation and trial can be places where God works deeply in our hearts. The desert also reminds us that Israel, alone and destitute, had to learn to trust the Lord — a lesson still relevant for those seeking God beyond appearances and comfort.

sens: Destroy a region, a city, causing ruin and desolation
Deprive someone of their possessions, strip them bare
Reduce to nothing, annihilate a structure or power
G2049.detail:
1. In the physical and geographical sense, to devastate means to destroy a region or a city, reducing it to ruin. It is the image of land being ravaged, of homes being destroyed. In Revelation 18:19, Babylon the great city is "destroyed" in one hour: all its wealth, all its structure collapses.
2. In the sense of stripping or removing goods: in Revelation 17:16, the ten horns "will strip" the prostitute of what she possesses, will expose her, will eat her flesh. It is to take away, to seize, to plunder.
3. In the figurative and moral sense, the word denotes the annihilation of a power, a unity, or an established order. When Jesus says, "Every kingdom divided against itself is devastated" (Matthew 12:25, Luke 11:17), He means that a house or kingdom in internal disagreement collapses, destroys itself from within. Division leads to inevitable ruin.
G2049.origine: The word comes from the Greek erēmos ("desert," "desolate," "empty"). The suffix -oō indicates an action that renders something in that state: to make desolate, to make empty. It thus signifies the transition from a state of order and habitation to a state of ruin, abandonment, emptiness. The root conveys the idea of devastation that leaves a place uninhabitable and empty.
G2049.emploi: The verb appears five times in the New Testament, concentrated mainly in Revelation. Jesus uses it twice in parallel (Matthew and Luke) to teach that a house or kingdom divided collapses: it is a spiritual and moral law. Revelation uses it to describe eschatological ruin: Babylon is destroyed (18:19), and the prostitute is stripped by the beast (17:16). In these passages, the word carries the weight of divine condemnation on a power hostile to God. The meaning varies according to the context: territorial destruction and moral destruction converge there.
G2049.portee: This word reminds the reader that internal division, deep disagreement, destroys any human structure — family, community, kingdom. Jesus teaches it as a permanent truth: unity is a condition for survival. In Revelation, He announces that God will ultimately destroy the rebellious powers that ravage the world. For the Christian, it is a call to unity in the body of Christ, and a certainty that the Lord will not allow evil to triumph.

sens: State of ruin and abandonment of a ravaged place
Systematic destruction of a city or sanctuary
Abomination that desecrates a holy place
G2050.detail:
1. Desolation is the state of ruin and abandonment that a place finds itself in after being ravaged. It is the result of destruction: the walls are torn down, the inhabitants have fled, everything is silent and empty. When Jerusalem is besieged by armies (Luke 21:20), its desolation is near — soon it will be uninhabitable and destroyed.

2. The word also refers to the act of destruction itself, the systematic ravaging of a city or sanctuary. It is a process of pillaging: fortifications are destroyed, lands are ravaged, holy places are desecrated. The Bible speaks of it as something that is fulfilled, that happens at a specific moment in history.

3. In a religious context, desolation takes on a particular meaning: it is the abomination of desolation (Matthew 24:15, Mark 13:14), an abominable desecration of God's sanctuary. The impious idol or sacrilege established in the Temple constitutes this desolation that evokes horror because it defiles the most sacred place in Israel.
G2050.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb « erēmoō » which means « to make desolate ». It is formed from the root « erēmos » (desert, abandonment). This evokes the image of a fertile and inhabited place becoming a barren and empty desert. The Hebrew Bible uses the words « shāmēm » (to become desolate) and « ḥorbāh » (ruin) for this same concept, reinforcing the idea of total and irreversible destruction.
G2050.emploi: This word appears three times in the New Testament, always in Jesus' teachings about the end times. In Matthew 24:15 and Mark 13:14, Jesus refers to Daniel's prophecy by speaking of the « abomination of desolation » established in the sanctuary: it is a sacrilegious violation of the Temple that announces its judgment. The nuance is that of a religious sacrilege, not merely a military destruction. In Luke 21:20, the context is slightly different: Jesus says that the desolation of Jerusalem is near when armies are seen besieging it. Here, desolation is the direct consequence of the siege and destruction of the city. The word thus applies both to the desecration of the Temple and to the total ruin of Jerusalem.
G2050.portee: Understanding this word helps to grasp the seriousness of Jesus' warnings. The abomination of desolation is not an ordinary destruction, but a sacrilegious desecration that triggers God's judgment. For disciples of all times, this word serves as a reminder that God does not indefinitely tolerate the violation of His sanctuary and idolatry, and that He acts in history to defend His holiness. It is a call to spiritual vigilance and repentance.

sens: Express disagreement, refuse to acknowledge a statement
Argue with disputes and quarrels, seek to be right at all costs
G2051.detail:
1. To contest means to express disagreement, to refuse to accept what is said to us. In Matthew 12:19, the Servant of the Lord « will not contest »: He will not argue to defend His honor or rights, even in the face of accusations.
2. The word also evokes disputes and quarrels where each seeks to impose their point of view. It is a refusal of peace, a desire to triumph rather than to yield. The context of a crowd accusing Jesus shows that there is tension, a possible confrontation.
G2051.origine: The word comes from the Greek ἔρις (éris), which means « quarrel » or « dispute ». This family expresses the idea of friction, of conflict between people. The root evokes agitation, clash. In the Greek Old Testament, the word translates Hebrew verbs expressing rebellion or transgression (such as מָרָה, marâ, to rebel).
G2051.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament: in Matthew 12:19. It is used in the negative future (« will not contest ») to describe the attitude of Christ according to the prophecy of Isaiah 42:2. Jesus, although confronted with opposition and accusations, does not defend His cause through dispute or aggressive argument. It is a characteristic of the suffering Servant: measured silence rather than quarrel.
G2051.portee: This word invites the Christian to contemplate the gentleness and humility of Christ in the face of unjust accusation. It reminds us that defending the truth does not always mean arguing, contesting, or seeking to win by words. Sometimes, it is the confident silence in God that testifies most powerfully.

sens: personal ambition seeking power and influence
selfish pursuit of one's own advantage
rivalry between individuals or groups
division and discord it provokes
quarrel motivated by personal interests
G2052.detail:
1. It is primarily personal ambition — that of someone who thinks only of their own prestige and dominating others. In Philippians 2:3, Paul urges Christians to do nothing from « spirit of faction », that is, without being guided by this selfish desire to appear or to be right.
2. It is also the « cabal », that is, a clique, a faction organized to advance the interests of one group at the expense of others. In 2 Corinthians 12:20, Paul fears finding in the church these « cabals » that divide believers.
3. The word also refers to the covert or declared rivalry between individuals. In Galatians 5:20, it appears among the sins of division: quarrels, jealousies, animosities, disputes — a list of interpersonal conflicts.
4. More broadly, it is the disorder and moral disturbance that follow: James 3:16 says that where this spirit reigns, there is disorder and all sorts of evil actions. It is a dynamic: selfishness breeds discord, which destroys peace.
G2052.origine: The Greek word comes from the root meaning « to seek for oneself ». In ancient Greek, it originally referred to task-oriented work, then zeal for oneself, personal ambition. The New Testament takes up this word to highlight how self-love, when not purified by the Spirit, transforms into internal struggle and division.
G2052.emploi: The word appears six times in the New Testament, always in the context of vices that destroy the unity of the church. Paul mentions it when he lists the sins that arise from the flesh (Galatians 5:20) or the disorders threatening the communities he visited (2 Corinthians 12:20). He regularly associates it with jealousy, quarrels, and pride, thus forming a coherent family of faults. In James, the « spirit of dispute » appears linked to a « bitter zeal » — a passion diverted from its true purpose — and it serves to illustrate how carnal wisdom provokes disorder (James 3:14, 16).
G2052.portee: This word calls the Christian to examine their heart: am I driven by the desire to be recognized, to be right at all costs, or by the love of Christ and my brothers? The spirit of faction poisons local churches by making each person a competitor rather than a collaborator. Paul and James invite us to uproot this selfish ambition through humility and the wisdom from above, which seeks peace, not personal victory.

sens: Textile fiber obtained from the fleece of sheep
White and soft color or appearance, like that of wool
G2053.detail:
1. Wool is the fiber that is taken from the fleece of sheep. It is a fabric that the ancients used to make clothing and textiles. In Hebrews 9:19, Moses uses scarlet wool (dyed red) to perform a purification rite, associating it with blood and hyssop — materials that Jewish law considered suitable for purification. Wool was a common and valuable material in antiquity.
2. With its white, soft, and fluffy appearance, wool evokes purity and whiteness. This is why John, in Revelation 1:14, describes the hair of Christ as "white like white wool, like snow": this image expresses the holiness, majesty, and eternity of the Son of God. The whiteness of wool symbolizes immortality and heavenly glory.
G2053.origine: The Greek word ἔριον (erion) simply means wool, textile fiber. It corresponds in Hebrew to the word צֶמֶר (tsemer), used in the Old Testament to describe the same material (see Leviticus 13:47 where wool is mentioned among unclean fabrics). The word is ancient and universal: every people working with wool called this fiber by that name.
G2053.emploi: The word appears twice in the New Testament, both in important visions or rituals. In Hebrews 9:19, it refers to the scarlet wool used in the rite of the first covenant — a legal and cultic act that seals the contract between God and Israel. In Revelation 1:14, it describes the white hair of Christ in his heavenly vision, associated with his majesty and eternity. Both uses highlight the solidity and nobility of wool.
G2053.portee: For the believer, the scarlet wool of Hebrews 9:19 reminds us that the old covenant rested on shed blood, a material purification that foreshadowed the sacrifice of Christ. The whiteness of the wool in Revelation 1:14 invites contemplation of the holiness of the Risen One and the hope of sharing in his immortal glory one day.

sens: Dispute, verbal conflict between people
Disagreement that creates tension and hostility
State of division or antagonism characterized by rivalry
G2054.detail: 1. A quarrel is a dispute or verbal confrontation between people, an exchange of harsh and conflicting words. This is the word Paul uses in Romans 1:29 to list sins, placing quarrel among the major vices alongside malice and deceit. 2. More broadly, a quarrel refers to the state of tension and hostility that arises when people disagree. In 1 Corinthians 3:3, Paul reproaches the Corinthians for being carnal precisely because there is jealousy and quarrels among them — the quarrel reveals that the community is not walking according to the Spirit. 3. In the context of lists of sins and moral faults (Galatians 5:20, 2 Corinthians 12:20), quarrel is an indicator of spiritual division: it manifests the absence of peace and unity. It directly opposes Christian values of harmony and brotherly love.
G2054.origine: The Greek word eris comes from a root evoking contention, struggle, or even personal rivalry. It literally denotes the conflict that arises between two opposing wills. The family of the word includes terms related to dispute and antagonism. In Psalms 139:20 and in other Greek texts of the Old Testament, the word appears to translate the Hebrew idea of litigation and dispute.
G2054.emploi: Eris appears 9 times in the New Testament, primarily in Paul's epistles. It falls into three main categories: first as a moral vice in catalogs of sins (Romans 1:29; Galatians 5:20; 2 Corinthians 12:20), where it is associated with envy, jealousy, and malice; second as a symptom of spiritual weakness in communities (1 Corinthians 1:11 and 3:3, where Paul is concerned about the quarrels among the Corinthians); finally in contexts of pastoral warning (1 Timothy 6:4, Titus 3:9). The word is often in the plural, emphasizing repeated and destructive quarrels. Paul systematically opposes it to spiritual maturity and unity in the church.
G2054.portee: For Paul, a quarrel is never a neutral or trivial act: it is a serious sin that betrays the state of the heart and destroys the Christian community. For the modern reader, this word reminds us that even verbal disputes, personal antagonisms, and relational tensions count as works of the flesh. Recognizing quarrel as sin invites us to actively seek peace, forgiveness, and reconciliation rather than personal victory.

sens: young goat or goat in general
impure or rejected creature (figurative sense)
G2055.detail:
1. A goat is a young male of the goat species, or the adult goat in general — a common domesticated animal in the Middle East. In Matthew 25:33, Jesus speaks of the sheep placed on the right and the goats on the left on the day of judgment: an image that contrasts two groups.
2. In this parable of judgment, the goat becomes the image of one who is rejected, separated from God, in contrast to the sheep which symbolizes the accepted elect. It is not that the goat is bad in itself, but its placement on the left (the side of judgment) gives it spiritual significance: the one who has not loved their neighbor will be set apart like the goat from the flock.
G2055.origine: The word ἐρίφιον (eriphion) is the diminutive of the Greek ἔριφος (eriphos), which means "goat" or "kid." It is a common language word that simply refers to the animal in the pastoral reality of the ancient world. The diminutive form does not make the animal smaller in meaning — it is simply the form that Greek uses for this familiar term.
G2055.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Matthew 25:33, in the parable of the final judgment. Jesus describes the king separating the nations "as a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats." The goats are not presented as wicked creatures, but as the group that will be placed on the left, rejected, while the sheep will be on the right, accepted. This simple and striking image, drawn from the rural life of Galilee, makes the final judgment concrete: a clear and definitive separation.
G2055.portee: This image of the goat helps the reader understand the reality and inevitability of the final judgment. It teaches that the separation between the elect and the reprobate will be as clear and visible as a separation between two flocks of animals. It also invites reflection: how will I be judged? Have I loved the little ones, the hungry, the prisoners? For it is not the goat itself that is condemned, but the one who has refused the love of their neighbor.

sens: Young goat, domesticated animal
Symbol of sin or guilt in divine judgment
G2056.detail:
1. A chevreau is a young buck or young goat, a domesticated animal raised for its meat and milk. It is a small livestock animal, smaller and less valuable than a sheep. In Matthew 25:32, Christ uses it to represent those who will be judged and condemned: "He will separate them one from another, as a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats."
2. Through the image of judgment, the chevreau symbolizes one who deserves condemnation, one whose guilt is established. The elder son in the parable (Luke 15:29) asks for a chevreau to feast with his friends, not to honor his father, but for his own satisfaction—showing a heart far from heaven. In this context, the chevreau represents the deserved reward of faithful work, but also the absence of grace toward the one who returns.
G2056.origine: The Greek word ἔριφος (eriphos) simply refers to the young of a goat. It comes from the group of Greek words for grazing animals, and it translates the Hebrew גְּדִי (gedi, young goat or kid). It is a common word in everyday Greek, without original mystical nuance: it names an animal that was raised in the Mediterranean and the Near East.
G2056.emploi: The word appears twice in the New Testament, always in the Gospels. In Matthew 25:32, Jesus uses it in the final judgment: the goats (that is, male goats, translated here as "goats") are separated from the sheep, an image of the final fate of the wicked. In Luke 15:29, the elder son asks for a chevreau to feast, expressing his resentment toward the father who has received the prodigal son. In both cases, the chevreau is an animal of little value, signifying a modest reward or a creature destined for judgment.
G2056.portee: This image reminds us that God's judgment clearly distinguishes those who belong to Him (the sheep) from those who resist Him (the goats). It also calls us to examine our hearts: are we, like the elder son, more concerned about our rights and rewards than about grace? The chevreau speaks to us of the cost of sin and the importance of mercy.

sens: Christian from Rome mentioned by Paul
G2057.detail: Hermas is a believer from the Christian community in Rome to whom the apostle Paul sends greetings in his letter to the Romans. He is listed among a group of faithful disciples that Paul wishes to honor personally (Romans 16:14).
G2057.origine: The name Hermas is the Doric form of the Greek Hermes, the name of the messenger god in Greek mythology. Among the Romans converted to Christ, this purely Greek name was borne by an ordinary believer, with no connection to idolatrous worship: it simply designates a man of that name, integrated into the community of saints.
G2057.emploi: Hermas appears only once in the New Testament, in Romans 16:14, where Paul names him among the Christians in Rome whom he greets. Paul also mentions "the brothers who are with [him]", indicating that Hermas belongs to a group of faithful who gather together, probably around a house church. This brief mention shows that Paul personally knew the local leaders and important believers in Rome, despite not having yet visited the city.

sens: Action of clarifying the meaning of a word, text, or foreign language
The result of this action: the meaning revealed, the explanation given
In the early Church, a spiritual gift enabling the understanding and explanation of words spoken in an unknown language
G2058.detail:
1. Interpretation is the action of translating or explaining what is not immediately understood. It is making clear what is obscure or in a foreign language. In 1 Corinthians 12:10, it is listed among the gifts of the Holy Spirit: "to another, the interpretation of tongues," meaning the ability to understand and explain words spoken in a language unknown to the assembly.
2. Interpretation can also refer to the result of this action: the explanation itself, the meaning made intelligible. It is what is stated, what comes from the mouth of the interpreter.
3. In the life of the Church, this spiritual gift complements the gift of speaking in tongues: while some receive the gift of expressing themselves in languages that the assembly does not understand, others receive the gift of interpreting, so that the entire assembly may be edified (1 Corinthians 14:26).
G2058.origine: The word comes from the verb ἑρμηνεύω (hermēneuô), which means "to explain, translate, interpret." This verb is itself linked to Hermes, the messenger of the gods in Greek mythology, who carries and transmits divine messages. The root thus evokes the idea of carrying a message, communicating it in a comprehensible way. The word is used in the Septuagint (Greek translation of the Old Testament) as early as Sirach.
G2058.emploi: This word appears twice in the New Testament, exclusively in Paul’s writings in 1 Corinthians, where he describes a specific spiritual gift in the early Church. In 1 Corinthians 12:10, it is included in the list of manifestations of the Holy Spirit, distinguished from other gifts as a particular ability. In 1 Corinthians 14:26, Paul reaffirms its importance for the edification of the assembly, emphasizing that everything must serve to build up when the community gathers. In these two passages, interpretation specifically applies to the understanding of "tongues"—that is, words spoken in languages that the listener does not naturally know.
G2058.portee: For the Christian, this word reminds us that the Holy Spirit is not only a source of prophetic words or spectacular manifestations, but also of understanding and clarity. It emphasizes that in communal life, discernment and explanation—making comprehensible what might remain obscure—are just as important as inspiration itself. It is an invitation not to seek "spectacular" gifts for their own sake, but to desire what truly edifies the Church.

sens: Explain the meaning of a word or term
Provide the translation or interpretation of a name
Reveal what something means or designates
G2059.detail:
1. To explain the meaning of a word or term: it is to clearly convey what something signifies. For example, in John 1:42, Jesus explains that the name "Cephas" means "Peter"—he translates and unfolds the meaning of the Aramaic word, making it intelligible.
2. To provide the translation or interpretation of a name: to reveal what a name means or where it comes from. In John 9:7, it is explained that Siloam means "sent"—showing the reader the hidden meaning of the name of the place.
3. To reveal what something designates or symbolizes: to make known the deeper significance of a term or reality. In Hebrews 7:2, Melchizedek is called "king of righteousness according to the meaning of his name"—showing that his name expresses and carries a spiritual truth.
G2059.origine: The word comes from the Greek hermēn- ("interpreter," one who translates and explains). It is a verb that concerns the act of conveying meaning from one language or form to another, or making clear what was obscure. The biblical context of its uses shows that the word explains names: it "names" by stating what the name means.
G2059.emploi: The verb appears three times in the provided uses, always to illuminate a name or term. In John 1:42, Jesus himself gives the meaning of the name "Cephas". In John 9:7, the narrator explains the meaning of the name "Siloam". In Hebrews 7:2, it is shown that the name of Melchizedek expresses a theological reality (righteousness). Each time, the interpretation reveals a spiritual or symbolic depth hidden in the name.
G2059.portee: Understanding this verb invites the reader to see that names in Scripture are never devoid of meaning: they carry a truth, often prophetic or spiritual. Peter means "rock", Siloam means "sent", Melchizedek expresses righteousness and peace. It is a call to listen to Scripture by scrutinizing what names unfold, rather than treating them as mere labels.

sens: The god of commerce and travelers in Greek and Roman mythology
A Christian from Rome known to Paul
G2060G.detail:
1. Mercury (or Hermes in Greek) is the god of commerce, travelers, and messengers in Greco-Roman religion. In Lystra, when Paul heals a crippled man, the pagan crowd mistakes him for this god because he preaches the Gospel: they think that Mercury has incarnated to bring a divine message (Acts 14:12). This reflects how pagans interpreted miracles through the filter of their beliefs.
2. A Christian bearing this Greek name was known to Paul in Rome. Paul greets him in his letter to the Romans, showing that the name of a pagan god could be carried without scandal by a believer who may have renounced it upon becoming a disciple of Christ.
G2060G.origine: The name comes from the ancient Greek *Hermês*, linked to the root *hermê* ("boundary stone," "cairn"): the Greeks erected "herms," small statues of the god, at crossroads and property boundaries. This role as guardian of passages and messages made Hermes the god of communications. The Romans adopted him under the name Mercurius (hence the French "Mercure"), and associated him with their gods of commerce and profit.
G2060G.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 14:12, in a very specific context: in Lystra, the pagans witness the healing of a crippled man by Paul and deduce that it is a divine epiphany (an appearance). They attribute to Barnabas the role of Jupiter (the greatest of the gods) and to Paul that of Mercury (the divine messenger), "because he was the one who spoke." This erroneous identification shows how non-believers filtered God's acts through their mythology. The text uses this moment to illustrate the gap between true faith in Jesus and the superstitions of the ancient world.
G2060G.portee: This passage reminds us how easy it is to misunderstand the true origin of a work or a miracle. For the modern reader, it is an invitation to discern: not to confuse the servant with the Lord, and not to let the ideas of the world around us obscure our understanding of what God is truly doing. It is also a call to humility: Paul and Barnabas do not accept these false divine attributions, refusing to steal from God the glory that belongs only to Him.

sens: Deity of Greek mythology, messenger of the gods
Name borne by a Christian from Rome
G2060H.detail:
1. Hermes is the Greek god whom the Romans called Mercury. In mythology, he is the messenger of the gods, the one who guides souls and protects travelers and merchants. This is why, when Paul and Barnabas heal a crippled man in Lystra, the crowd takes them for gods and cries out: "The gods have come down to us," calling Paul "Mercury" (Acts 14:12).
2. Hermes is also the name of a Christian whom Paul greets in his letter to the Romans (Romans 16:14). This Greek name was borne by slaves and men of humble status; he is a simple disciple of the Lord among the brothers in Rome.
G2060H.origine: The Greek name "Hermes" comes from the verb meaning "to announce, to interpret" — the god is the divine messenger. In Greek mythology, Hermes guides the souls of the dead, protects travelers, and invents the art of cunning. The Greeks and Romans honored Hermes at crossroads and on hilltops with small statues called herms. This is not a Hebrew word: it is a Greco-Roman name that shows how Paul and his friends lived in a world where mythology was ever-present.
G2060H.emploi: The word "Hermes" appears only once in the Bible: in Romans 16:14, where it is a person's name, a Christian from Rome whom Paul greets by name. The context shows that Paul personally knows the converts from the capital, even those of humble status, and honors them by naming them. The use of the mythological name by a Christian does not indicate that he worships the gods: it was simply a common Greek name in the Roman Empire among all classes of the population.
G2060H.portee: This verse reminds us that the early Church was made up of ordinary people from all walks of life — slaves, workers, women, men of no importance in the eyes of the world. Paul knows them, greets them, and treats them as his brothers. It is a poignant image of the Church: no great figures, but faithful, modest believers, each with a name, each precious in the eyes of the apostle and of God.

sens: A Christian from Asia who abandoned the apostle Paul
G2061.detail: Hermogenes is a Christian mentioned only once in the New Testament. Paul refers to him in his second letter to Timothy, saying: "You know that all those in Asia have turned away from me, among whom are Phygellus and Hermogenes" (2 Timothy 1:15). He is a faithful one who, at the time when Paul is going through a difficult period, turned away from him, probably out of fear or lack of courage in the face of persecution.
G2061.origine: The name Hermogenes comes from Greek and means "born of Hermes" or "son of Hermes," the messenger god of ancient Greece. It is a name used in the Greco-Roman world, particularly in Asia Minor where many Christians lived. In the New Testament context, it is not the mythology that matters, but the fact that it is the name of a real Christian from the first century.
G2061.emploi: Hermogenes appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Timothy 1:15. Paul writes this letter toward the end of his life, presumably while in prison in Rome, and he lists the Christians from Asia who have abandoned him. Hermogenes is mentioned alongside Phygellus, suggesting that they may have acted together or that their defection was particularly notable. This brief but clear mention shows that even among converts, faithfulness was not automatic in the face of trials.
G2061.portee: The case of Hermogenes teaches the reader that Christian confession can be shaken by persecution or difficulties. His abandonment of Paul invites each believer to reflect on their own perseverance in faith: will I keep trusting God and His servants when everything becomes difficult? It is a call to authentic faithfulness, not a faithfulness that fades away as soon as the price to pay becomes too high.

sens: Animal qui se meut en rampant sur le sol
Créature vivante de petite taille, souvent méprisée
G2062.detail:
1. The reptile is an animal that crawls or drags itself on the ground — this is the primary image of the Greek word, which comes from the verb "to crawl." In Peter's vision (Acts 10:12), God lowers a sheet from heaven filled with "four-footed animals and reptiles of the earth": reptiles are included alongside other beasts as visible and terrestrial creatures.
2. More broadly, this word designates any living creature that is despised or considered inferior. In Romans 1:23, Paul denounces those who worship idols in the form of reptiles instead of the true God: the reptile symbolizes what is lowly, lacking nobility. James 3:7 reminds us that "every kind of beast, bird, reptile, and sea creature" has been tamed by man: even the humblest creatures are subject to human nature.
G2062.origine: The Greek word comes from the verb meaning "to crawl," "to drag oneself." It is a very concrete image: the animal that moves by crawling on the ground, without legs or with very short legs. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, the word primarily corresponds to two terms designating everything that crawls or swarms, from the serpent to insects. The root evokes the undulating, almost visceral movement characteristic of these creatures.
G2062.emploi: The word "reptile" appears only four times in the New Testament. It is found in two parallel episodes (Acts 10 and 11) where Peter receives a vision dividing animals into categories: four-footed animals, wild beasts, reptiles, and birds. Paul uses it in Romans 1:23 to show the absurdity of those who confuse the worshiper with the worshiped, replacing God with representations of "reptile" animals. Finally, James uses it to affirm that even the smallest creatures have been tamed by man. The word remains attached to the idea of a crawling creature, often presented as one of the lowest categories of the animal kingdom.
G2062.portee: This word reminds us that the entire creation — even its most despised or repugnant creatures — is the work of God and belongs to Him. It serves as a warning against idolatry: worshiping an image of a reptile rather than the living God is one of the most absurd forms of human rebellion against divine truth. Finally, it emphasizes man's dominion over creation, a dominion that God established from the beginning.

sens: De la couleur du sang ou du feu
Qui est d'une teinte écarlate ou cramoisi
(Adjectif) : la mer Rouge, bras de mer entre l'Afrique et l'Asie
G2063.detail:
1. The word simply designates the color red, that of blood or fire — a bright and striking color. In the Hebrew Old Testament, the same root evokes the idea of redness or scarlet hue.

2. In Acts 7:36 and Hebrews 11:29, the expression "the Red Sea" (literally "the red sea") names the body of water that the Israelites crossed during the Exodus: this ancient name likely came from the particular redness of its waters or rocky shores, or from an association with a desert deity. It is the crucial place where God demonstrated His power by parting the waters and saving His people.
G2063.origine: The Greek word eruthros comes from an ancient root expressing redness or a reddish glow. It directly translates the Hebrew "adom" (אֱדֹם), which means red and can also refer to a land or a person with a reddish appearance. In the Greek Old Testament, this same adjective applies to the blood-stained garment of the Servant in Isaiah 63:2.
G2063.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, both in passages that recount or celebrate the Exodus. In Acts 7:36, Stephen mentions the miracle of crossing the Red Sea during the liberation from Egypt. In Hebrews 11:29, the author cites the same event as an exemplary act of faith: the Israelites crossed the sea on dry ground, while the Egyptians who tried to follow perished. In both cases, "the Red Sea" is a symbol of divine salvation and deliverance.
G2063.portee: The Red Sea reminds the Christian reader that God acts powerfully to save His people. This event, cited in the New Testament passages, encourages faith: just as the ancient Israelites saw God conquer the impossible, the believer can also trust in His power and salvation.

sens: Arriver en un lieu, y apparaître, en parlant d'une personne
Aller vers quelqu'un ou quelque part, se rendre
Arriver à un moment donné, en parlant d'un temps ou d'un événement
Apparaître publiquement, se manifester, en particulier du Messie et de Jésus
S'approcher, se présenter devant quelqu'un
G2064.detail:
1. The most common meaning: a person arrives or comes to a place. The Magi "come" from the East to worship the king (Matthew 2:2), or someone "comes" to Jesus from afar to be healed. It is simply a movement from one point to another.

2. Coming to someone with an intention, going to meet them. The disciples "come" to Jesus, or Jesus "comes" to us (John 14:23). The emphasis is on the relationship established by this movement.

3. A moment or event that "comes" means that it arrives, that it occurs in time. "Days will come" when the disciples will mourn (Matthew 9:15). It is the arrival of an era, of a time.

4. Coming to public light, manifesting, especially when speaking of the Messiah who "comes" into the world or of Jesus who "will come" again (Matthew 11:3, Matthew 10:23). The image is that of something appearing, revealing itself.

5. Coming to someone, approaching them, often for a service or a request. The disciples "come" to Jesus with questions, the sick to be healed.
G2064.origine: The verb ἔρχομαι is very ancient in Greek. In the Old Testament translated into Greek, it often renders the Hebrew בּוֹא (bo'a), which literally means "to enter, to penetrate," an image of crossing a threshold or a limit. It also translates הלךְ (halak), "to go, to walk." The Greek verb primarily evokes the concrete movement of the body that moves, and then everything that "sets in motion" in time or space.
G2064.emploi: This word is extremely frequent in the New Testament (603 occurrences): it is one of the essential movement verbs. It appears in all the Gospels, the Acts, and the epistles. Matthew uses it 95 times, John 155 times. The meaning varies according to the context: "to come" for a physical arrival (Matthew 2:2), "to go" for a voluntary movement (Matthew 16:24, following Jesus), "to enter" for crossing a threshold (Matthew 9:28). With prepositions, it expresses nuances: "to come from" (where one comes from), "to come to" (to whom or what), "to come toward" (to approach). Its use regarding Jesus or the Messiah who "comes" is crucial: it is the expectation of a public manifestation, either at the beginning of the ministry (John 1:29) or at the second coming (1 Corinthians 4:5).
G2064.portee: This simple verb reminds the reader that God and Jesus "come" to men: it is the idea of condescension, of active presence. Whether Jesus "comes" to us or we "go" to Him, it is the same movement of encounter. The word also invites the believer to await the future coming of the Lord, not as a distant abstraction, but as an approaching event that changes present life.

sens: To ask a question, to inquire of someone
To request something from someone, to make a request
To plead, to implore insistently
To address a prayer to God
G2065.detail:
1. The most direct meaning is to ask someone a question to obtain information. Jesus questions his disciples: "Who do people say that I am?" (Matthew 16:13). The Pharisees also inquire about the way of life of those they encounter (John 9:15). It is a request for clarification or knowledge.

2. In late ancient Greek, this word took on the meaning of asking someone for something — a favor, an action, a service. A Pharisee "prays" Jesus to eat at his house (Luke 7:36), meaning he invites him insistently. A centurion "prays" the apostle Peter to come to him (Acts 10:48).

3. Affectionate insistence often marks this verb: when one prays someone, respect and urgency are intertwined. The disciples "pray" Jesus to stay with them (Luke 8:37) or to teach them (1 Thessalonians 5:12). It is less a simple request than a heartfelt plea.

4. In the relationship with God, this word becomes prayer in the fullest sense: Jesus says, "I pray for them" (John 17:9) speaking of his intercession before the Father. It is the act of addressing a request to God with respect and trust.
G2065.origine: The verb comes from a Greek root related to the idea of addressing someone. In the Greek Old Testament, it regularly translates the Hebrew "shaal" (שָׁאַל), which primarily means "to ask a question," then "to request, to require." The word emphasizes the relationship of the one who asks with the one being asked: it implies a relationship, a possible listening.
G2065.emploi: This verb appears about 61 times in the New Testament, mostly in the Gospels (particularly John and Luke) and in a few epistles. It primarily denotes the act of asking a question (Jesus questioning his disciples, the Pharisees interrogating the healed sick). Then it shifts towards the request and plea: inviting someone to one's home, asking for help, a favor. Finally, applied to the relationship with God, it takes on the noble meaning of intercessory prayer. The context and the complements (who is being questioned? what is being asked?) determine the exact meaning: inquiry, courteous request, or pious supplication.
G2065.portee: This word shows that Christian prayer begins with a relationship: that of the one who asks with the one who can respond. Whether it is to inquire, to implore, or to intercede, it is always to address someone with respect and trust. Prayer is not a monologue, but a dialogue. It also assumes that God, like a person, listens and has the power to respond. Finally, this verb reminds us that to pray is to dare to ask — which combines boldness and humility.

sens: Clothing worn by a person
External appearance marked by the quality or prestige of the clothing
Insignia or distinguishing signs of a charge or status
G2066.detail:
1. The word primarily designates simply clothing, the costume one wears. It is the visible garment one has on. Herod "clothed in his royal garments" (Acts 12:21) or the man who enters the assembly "with a splendid garment" (James 2:2) are concrete images: we speak of the fabric, of the appearance of the one who wears it.
2. By extension, the garment becomes a sign of what the person is socially. A "shining garment" (Acts 10:30) or "resplendent garments" (Luke 24:4) are no longer just fabrics: they reflect the dignity, wealth, or character of the one who wears them. This is why Herod wraps Jesus in "a shining garment" (Luke 23:11) as an insult: the ridiculous clothing underscores the contempt.
3. In King Herod "clothed in his royal garments," the clothing embodies his power and status (Acts 12:21). The garment becomes the symbol of authority or function.
G2066.origine: The Greek word ἐσθής comes from the verb ἕννυμι, which means "to clothe" or "to dress." It originally describes what dresses, what one puts on. It is a common word in ancient Greek to designate any clothing or costume. The root refers to the action of covering oneself, of dressing, and thus to both the practical act and what results: the garment that covers the body.
G2066.emploi: The word appears 7 times in the New Testament, almost always in a narrative of Luke or in James. Each time it is a visible, remarkable garment. In Luke, the garment often shines or resplendently: the two men at the tomb in "resplendent garments" (Luke 24:4), the angel in "a shining garment" (Acts 10:30). Herod and his guards dress Jesus in "a shining garment" (Luke 23:11) to mock him. Herod himself appears "clothed in his royal garments," which emphasizes his splendor and power. James uses it to contrast the one who enters "with a splendid garment" to the one who is "poorly dressed" (James 2:2-3), showing how garments reveal and reinforce social inequalities. Each time, the garment is never neutral: it speaks of dignity, power, or inequality.
G2066.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that our appearances — our clothing, our external status — never convey our true value in the eyes of God. Jesus, clothed in a shining garment in mockery, and the one who "clothes the poor," invites us to see beyond the garments. James' teaching on the rich and the poor warns the church not to judge by appearance. It is also a sign: the angels in the Gospel wear resplendent garments, signs of the divine presence, which speaks to the heart of the reader and directs their gaze toward heaven.

sens: To consume food for nourishment
To share a meal with others
To observe a religious commandment by eating (Passover, Lord's Supper)
To consume, to devour, to destroy
G2068.detail:
1. The fundamental meaning: to consume food to live. It is the simple act of eating bread, meat, food. Jesus says to his disciples in Matthew 14:21: "Those who had eaten were about five thousand men" — the physical act of nourishing oneself after a day with him.
2. Sharing a meal creates a social bond and signifies friendship or hospitality. When Jesus "eats with tax collectors" in Matthew 9:11, the Pharisees are scandalized: eating with someone means recognizing them as worthy of the table. The verb often appears in these table scenes (Mark 14:18, Luke 10:7).
3. The verb also applies to specific religious acts: eating the Passover (Matthew 26:26 at the last supper), eating the Lord's Supper in 1 Corinthians 11:28. Here, "eating" becomes an act laden with divine significance.
4. By figurative extension, the verb means "to devour" or "to consume" — an image of destruction. Revelation 17:16 speaks of peoples who will "devour" a woman, meaning they will destroy her.
G2068.origine: The verb comes from an ancient root that evokes the absorption of food. In Hebrew, the main word translated is אכל (akal), which has exactly the same meaning: to eat, to consume. The family of the Greek word also includes terms for "food" (τροφή) and "meal" (δεῖπνον). The basic image is physical and concrete: to introduce food into one's mouth and absorb it.
G2068.emploi: The verb appears 55 times in the New Testament, mostly in the Gospels and in 1 Corinthians. The usages can be divided into four categories. First, ordinary food: the disciples "eat" grain on the Sabbath (Luke 6:1), Jesus "eats" fish after his resurrection (Luke 24:42 according to other witnesses).
