Next, social meals: eating with someone marks acceptance (Matthew 9:11 where Jesus eats with tax collectors). Then, religious rites: eating the Passover before the crucifixion (Matthew 26:26), eating the Lord's Supper in 1 Corinthians 11:20-28, where eating unworthily brings judgment upon oneself. Finally, the figurative use: in 1 Corinthians 10:31 "whether you eat or drink... do all for the glory of God," the simple act of eating becomes an act of worship.
G2068.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that physical life — nourishing oneself, sharing a table — is both real and sacred. Jesus "eats" to show us that he truly incarnated; he eats with the outcasts to accept the rejected. The Lord's Supper, where we "eat" bread, unites the ordinary gesture with communion with the Risen One. Finally, the lesson of 1 Corinthians 10:31 invites the believer to live every act, even the simplest, in the presence of God.

sens: ancestor of Jesus in the genealogy of Luke
G2069.detail: Esli is a man mentioned only once in the Bible, in the genealogy of Jesus according to Luke. He is the father of Nahum and the son of Naggaï (Luke 3:25). This genealogy traces back from Jesus to Adam and shows that Jesus is part of the continuity of the history of the people of Israel. Esli is one of those many ancestors of whom we know nothing more than the name: the Bible recounts no events of his life, but places him in the chain of generations that led to the birth of the Messiah.
G2069.origine: The name Esli appears only in the Greek text of the New Testament. Its Hebrew origin is uncertain. It appears in Luke's genealogy as a link in the long chain of Jesus' ancestors, tracing back through David to Adam. It is a proper name of a real person in the history of Israel, although no external sources have preserved any trace of him.
G2069.emploi: Esli appears only once in the Bible, in Luke 3:25, at the heart of the genealogy of Jesus. He is presented as the father of Nahum, who is himself the father of Amos. This genealogy, which Luke traces from Jesus to Adam, lists ancestors for the most part unknown in biblical history. Their enumeration emphasizes that the coming of Jesus is not an isolated event, but the culmination of a history of salvation that spans generations. Esli thus represents one of those millions of ordinary men who formed the people from which the Messiah was promised.

sens: Object made of glass or polished metal that reflects the image of the one looking into it
Imperfect or veiled image of something
Representation or reflection of divine reality
G2072.detail:
1. A mirror is an object that reflects physical image: in James 1:23, the man who listens to the Word without putting it into practice "looks in a mirror at his natural face," then goes away and forgets what he saw — the reflected image disappears as soon as one turns away from the mirror.
2. The mirror can symbolize an imperfect or blurred vision of reality: in 1 Corinthians 13:12, Paul says that we see "through a mirror, dimly" — this is an image that speaks of our limited and veiled knowledge of the things of God in this present life.
3. By extension, the mirror represents what allows us to know or see something that is not directly accessible to us: our current understanding of God and His plan comes through an imperfect reflection, unlike the direct vision "face to face" that we will have in eternity.
G2072.origine: The Greek word ἔσοπτρον comes from the root meaning "to look" or "to see." It is an object from everyday ancient life: mirrors of the Greco-Roman era were made of bronze or polished metal, which explains why the image is less clear and precise than in our modern mirrors. The word appears only twice in the New Testament, but the image of the mirror was already present in the Greek Old Testament to speak of reflection and knowledge.
G2072.emploi: The word appears twice in the New Testament, each time with a slightly different meaning. In James 1:23, the mirror is concrete and literal: a man looks into it and sees his face as it is, but immediately forgets that vision — it is a comparison to show that the Word heard without obedience does not change the one who listens. In 1 Corinthians 13:12, the mirror becomes a theological image: Paul uses it to say that our current knowledge of God is like that which one would have by looking in a dim mirror — indirect, partial, enigmatic. Both uses exploit the imperfect nature of the mirror's reflection: in one case, one does not retain what one has seen; in the other, one cannot see clearly.
G2072.portee: These two images of the mirror teach the Christian two important truths: first, that the Word heard must produce a concrete transformation — it is not enough to know the truth, one must practice it and allow it to change our lives. Secondly, that our current knowledge of God, as real as it is, remains always limited and incomplete — we see only "in a riddle," and we must have the humility to recognize that we will truly know only in eternity, face to face with our Lord.

sens: Time of day when the sun sets, between day and night
End of a period, approach of a conclusion
G2073.detail:
1. The evening is the time of day when sunlight declines and night falls. It is marked by increasing darkness and the approach of rest. In Luke 24:29, the disciples urge Jesus to stay "for the evening is approaching, the day is now far spent": they recognize that the light is fading and that night would make travel difficult. In Acts 4:3, the apostles are thrown into prison "for it was already evening": night prevents the authorities from acting further. In Acts 28:23, Paul speaks of Jesus "from morning till evening": a whole day of intense conversation, from dawn to dusk.
2. Figuratively, the evening can evoke the end of a period, the approach of a conclusion or fulfillment, as the end of the day symbolizes a transition to a new phase.
G2073.origine: The Greek word hespéra comes from the adjective hespéros ("belonging to the evening, western"). It literally designates the moment when the sun tilts toward the west. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, evening is called ‛ârâb, which also means "west," since it is toward the west that the sun sets. The Greek hespéra carries the same dual meaning: it marks both the time of day and the geographical direction.
G2073.emploi: This word appears three times in the New Testament, solely in the Gospels and Acts. It always designates the concrete moment of evening, the end of the natural day. In Luke (24:29), evening is a practical reason to stay: night is approaching and travel becomes perilous. In Acts (4:3 and 28:23), evening marks either a temporal limit of imprisonment or the duration of a conversation. Each time, it is about evening as an observable and relevant fact for the action described in the text.
G2073.portee: Understanding that evening in the Bible is never a mere ornament: it is a moment that organizes life, movements, rest, and even imprisonment. For the Christian, evening can remind us that each day has an end, that time flows, and that we must learn to welcome moments of rest and intimacy — like the disciples who ask Jesus to stay with them as evening falls.

sens: Ancestor of Jesus in the genealogy of David
G2074.detail: 1. Esrom is a man from the Old Testament, a direct ancestor of Jesus according to the Davidic lineage. He appears in the genealogy of Matthew 1:3 where he is presented as the son of Pharès and the father of Aram, and in that of Luke 3:33 with the same genealogical position. He is a character who embodies the link between Judah and David, helping to establish that Jesus is indeed a descendant of the tribe of Judah and the promised royalty.
G2074.origine: Esrom comes from the Hebrew name Hetsron (חֶצְרוֹן), attested in the Old Testament in Genesis 46:12, Numbers 26:21, and 1 Chronicles 2. The Hebrew word literally means "fortified village" or "enclosure." It is a name that carries the history of the people of Israel and remains important in the messianic genealogy translated by the Septuagint and taken up by the Greek evangelists.
G2074.emploi: Esrom appears only twice in the New Testament, solely in the genealogies of Jesus. In Matthew 1:3, he is listed in the genealogy of Joseph (the adoptive father of Jesus according to Matthew), as a link in the chain connecting Judah to David. In Luke 3:33, he appears in the genealogy of Jesus according to Luke, in a list that traces back to Adam. In both cases, his role is purely genealogical: to establish that Jesus legally descends from the royal lineage of Judah, ensuring that he is indeed the promised Messiah, heir to the throne of David.
G2074.portee: For the Christian reader, Esrom reminds us that Jesus is rooted in a real and verifiable history, not in a myth. The presence of Esrom's name (and all biblical ancestors) in the Gospel affirms that the incarnation of the Son of God is grounded in the history of Israel and in the promises made to David. It is an invitation to see that God governs history over entire generations to fulfill His plan of salvation.

sens: Who comes at the end of a series, after all others in order or time
Who occupies the lowest position, the least honorable or least important
Who is distant or extreme in space
Who characterizes the end times, the ultimate moment in the history of the world
Who concerns the final judgment or the resurrection of the dead at the end of times
G2078.detail:
1. The one who comes after all others in a succession: this is the opposite of the first. Jesus says, "I tell you the truth, you will not get out of there until you have paid the last penny" (Matthew 5:26): the last coin, the one that is paid last. Or in the order of time: "Some are last who will be first, and some are first who will be last" (Luke 13:30), announcing a divine reversal.
2. The one who is in the last rank, the most despised or least esteemed. Paul says: "God has made us, apostles, the last of men, condemned to death in a way" (1 Corinthians 4:9), evoking the shame and apparent indignity of their status in the eyes of the world.
3. Who is located at the extremity or end: "the last day, the great day of the feast" (John 7:37) refers to the final day of the celebration.
4. Who belongs to the last days before the return of Christ and the end of the world. "You have hoarded treasures in the last days" (James 5:3) speaks of the present time as that which precedes fulfillment. "God, after speaking long ago to our fathers by the prophets, has spoken to us in these last days by His Son" (Hebrews 1:2) places the coming of Christ in history.
5. Who concerns the final renewal: "I am the Alpha and the Omega, the first and the last" (Revelation 1:17) is applied to Christ as the one who encompasses all times and will command the final resurrection: "I, the Alpha and the Omega, the first and the last" (Revelation 22:13).
G2078.origine: The Greek word eschatos comes from an Indo-European root meaning the extremity or end. In Hebrew, the Greek Old Testament uses this word to translate notably aharon and ahérit, which literally mean "the one who comes after" and "end, back." The family of the Greek word includes variants to express order or position in a sequence. It is a fundamental word in Christian eschatological vocabulary, that is, one that speaks of the ultimate fulfillment of history according to God.
G2078.emploi: The word appears 49 times in the New Testament, primarily in the four Gospels, Paul, and Revelation. In Matthew and Mark, it often designates order or rank ("Matthew 20:8": the master pays the vineyard workers starting with the last ones). In Luke, it carries a moral or spiritual nuance: the reversal of values ("Luke 13:30"). John uses it for eschatology, the final resurrection: "I will raise him up at the last day" (John 6:39-40). Paul uses it theologically: Christ is "the firstfruits, then those who belong to Christ at His coming. Then comes the end" (1 Corinthians 15:23-26), marking the order of final events. Revelation takes up this language to describe Christ as "the first and the last" (Revelation 1:17, 2:8, 22:13), affirming His sovereignty over all time.
G2078.portee: This word invites the Christian to grasp that history is not without direction: it tends toward a fulfillment desired by God. It comforts by promising that those who are despised now may be first in the eyes of God (Luke 13:30). It also warns: the last days are approaching, time is passing, judgment will come (James 5:3; 1 John 2:18). Finally, it affirms that Christ masters the beginning and the end of all — an assurance for the believer's heart amid upheavals.

sens: At the point of dying, in imminent danger of death
In a desperate or critical situation
G2079.detail:
1. The word describes someone who is at the extreme limit of life, on the verge of death. It expresses mortal danger: Jairus' daughter is gravely ill, and her father comes to plead with Jesus, saying she is "at the extreme" (Mark 5:23), meaning she has almost no human hope of survival.
2. More broadly, the word can apply to any situation pushed to its limits, where there is only one step left before the fatal outcome. It is a vivid way of expressing absolute urgency and the extremity of need.
G2079.origine: The word comes from the Greek root *eschatos*, which means "last" or "extreme," the same root found in "eschatology" (the study of last things). The adverb formed from this adjective intensifies this idea of extremity: not just an extreme point, but the state of being pushed to the extreme. In Hebrew, the idea is often rendered by expressions like "in very bad condition" or "at death."
G2079.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Mark 5:23. It is the moment when Jairus, a synagogue leader, falls at Jesus' feet to entrust his dying daughter to Him. The use of the term "extreme" emphasizes the urgency of the case and justifies divine intervention: the child can only be saved by a miracle, as she has reached the last moment. It is a rare expression in biblical Greek, used mainly in the dramatic context of serious illnesses and desperate situations.
G2079.portee: This word reminds the reader that Jesus is confronted with the extreme limits of our human condition: serious illness, imminent death, parental despair. By using this strong term, Mark highlights the reality of the drama and prepares the reader's heart to receive the miracle that will follow. Jairus' faith is manifested by coming to seek Jesus precisely when everything seems lost — that is where the power of God is exercised.

sens: Inside a closed space, in the interior of a place
The deep and hidden part of a person, their intimate essence
G2080.detail:
1. The word first describes a physical closed or defined place, the space that is inside. When Peter follows Jesus, he goes "into the inner courtyard of the high priest" (Mark 14:54): he enters a closed space. Similarly, the disciples are locked "in the house" with the doors shut when Jesus joins them (John 20:26), and the guards seek the apostles "inside" the prison (Acts 5:23). It is the material, concrete interior.
2. By extension, the word designates what is deep within a being, hidden from the sight of others. Paul speaks of "the inner man" (Romans 7:22) to refer to the deep part of his conscience where he desires to obey God, distinct from what is seen on the outside. In 1 Corinthians 5:12, "those inside" contrasts with "those outside": it refers to the members of the Christian community, in contrast to the unbelievers who are separated from them.
G2080.origine: The word comes from a root meaning to enter or penetrate (itself related to "toward, in"). It is an ancient form of Greek, already aged at the time of the New Testament. The word is structurally opposed to "outside" (ἔξω): it always marks an interiority, a depth, a hidden or enclosed character. The central idea is that of crossing a boundary to enter a distinct space.
G2080.emploi: The word appears nine times in the New Testament. It is first used in a concrete and spatial sense: Peter enters the Temple courtyard, the disciples are locked in a house, the prison is closed. Then, it takes on a figurative and spiritual sense, particularly in Paul: "the inner man" becomes the seat of conscience, the true self, the deep moral and spiritual life, that which obeys God's law with all its heart. The transition from the first to the second meaning occurs naturally: from physical space to the inner space of the soul.
G2080.portee: This word invites the believer to distinguish between outward appearance and inner reality. Paul teaches us that it is "the inner man" who is renewed day by day by the grace of God (2 Corinthians 4:16), while the body ages. True obedience, true love do not reside in visible gestures, but in what is hidden from the eyes of men, in the depth of the heart. It is an invitation to cultivate our communion with God not to appear, but to be transformed from within.

sens: From the inside, originating from within
Inside, in a closed space
On the inner level, at the heart
What is hidden, secret, or invisible
G2081.detail:
1. "From the inside" indicates the source or origin: evil thoughts come from within, that is, from the hearts of men (Mark 7:21). It refers to what comes from within, emanating from a closed place or depth.
2. "Inside" simply designates the internal part of a place or object: the closed door, inside the house (Luke 11:7), or the eyes filled inside and out (Revelation 4:8).
3. "At the heart" or "internally" speaks of moral and spiritual life: the Pharisees are clean on the outside but full of impurities inside (Matthew 23:27), that is, in their deep being, their heart.
4. What is "inside" is hidden or invisible: the interior that only God truly knows. Jesus asks: did not the one who created the outside also create the inside? (Luke 11:40), revealing that God sees what is secret and inaccessible to men.
G2081.origine: The word comes from the preposition ἔσω (eso, "inside") and the suffix -θεν which marks origin or provenance. It thus primarily denotes the direction "from within" or "from the inside." In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, it often translates words like פָּנִים (panim, "face" or "inside") and בַּיִת (bayit, "house" or "inside"), which emphasize the idea of what is hidden, deep, or at the heart of something.
G2081.emploi: The word appears twelve times in the New Testament, mainly in Matthew, Mark, and Luke, and in Revelation. It is particularly frequent in Jesus' teachings on the contrast between outward appearance and the reality of the heart: false prophets are wolves "inside" (Matthew 7:15), the Pharisees are defiled "inside" even if they appear clean (Matthew 23:25-28). In Mark and Luke, "inside" refers to the human heart as the source of sin (Mark 7:21, 23) or hidden desire (Luke 11:39, 40). Revelation uses it to describe the inside of celestial beings filled with eyes (Revelation 4:8, 5:1). Paul uses it once to express a troubled inner condition (2 Corinthians 7:5). The word always denounces a hidden, invisible, or inner reality, in contrast to what is seen.
G2081.portee: This word invites the reader not to rely on appearances. Jesus uses it to show that what defiles a person is what comes out of their heart, not what they ingest from the outside. It reminds us that God scrutinizes the inside of the heart and thoughts: nothing escapes Him. For the Christian, this means that true transformation is first internal, from the heart, and that religious hypocrisy — being pure in appearance but corrupt inside — is one of Jesus' most severe critiques. It is a call to authenticity and spiritual sincerity.

sens: located inside, closer to the heart or center
that is hidden, withdrawn, secret
belonging to the soul, to the spirit rather than to the body
G2082.detail:
1. The primary meaning is spatial and concrete: what is located inside a place, away from the entrance or surface. In Acts 16:24, the "inner" prison is the deep cell of the dungeon, where the most dangerous prisoners are locked up — Paul and Silas are thrown in and chained to stocks. It is a prison within a prison, darker and harsher.

2. By extension, the word describes what is hidden, secret, withdrawn from sight. It is the image of the veil in Hebrews 6:19: our hope penetrates "beyond" the veil of the temple, entering into the most holy place where God dwells, invisible to men but real and certain.

3. Figuratively, "inner" qualifies what touches the soul, the deep spirit, in contrast to what is external or superficial. When our hope penetrates beyond the veil, it reaches the hidden spiritual reality, the invisible world of God Himself.
G2082.origine: The word comes from ἔσω ("inside", an Indo-European root meaning "inner"), and it is a comparative form that reinforces the idea of "even more inside." In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, the word פְּנִימִי ("inner") expresses the same idea of what is at the heart of a place or reality. The root evokes the image of penetrating deeper, seeking what is hidden at the center.
G2082.emploi: This word appears twice in the New Testament, once as an adjective in its full sense. In Acts 16:24, it describes a physical place, the inner prison of the dungeon — this is its concrete and literal use. In Hebrews 6:19, it is used in a more spiritual and figurative sense: hope penetrates "beyond" the veil of the sanctuary, that is, towards the very presence of God, the invisible and sacred beyond. This passage shows how the word shifts from the concrete to the spiritual: it always describes what is deep, hidden, withdrawn, but applied to the divine reality rather than to a building.
G2082.portee: This word reminds us that our Christian hope is not a mere illusion or vague feeling: it penetrates into the invisible and real world of God, beyond what our eyes see. Like an anchor that sinks deep to hold firm, our hope connects us to the eternal and certain reality of the heavenly sanctuary. It invites us to seek what is inner and lasting, beyond the appearances of the visible world.

sens: companion, mate
a person with whom one has a relationship of equality or familiarity
a term of courteous or ironic address
G2083.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a companion, someone who shares the same condition or group: a fellow traveler or worker. In Matthew 20:13, the master of the vineyard calls "friend" the one who has engaged with him by contract — he is a partner, someone equal in the agreement made.
2. It is also a way of addressing someone with a certain familiarity or cordiality. However, this term can take on an ironic or formal tone depending on the context: in Matthew 22:12, the address "my friend" precedes a question that reveals a transgression; in Matthew 26:50, Jesus uses it knowing that Judas is betraying him — the word then highlights the cruel contrast between the appearance of friendship and the reality of betrayal.
G2083.origine: The word comes from an ancient Greek root meaning "companion, mate." In the Greek Bible, it primarily translates the Hebrew "friend, close one" (רֵעַ). The word evokes the idea of sharing, of a relationship established between peers, rather than a deep friendship based on affection; this is why it is suitable for polite or contractual addresses.
G2083.emploi: The word appears three times in Matthew, always as a term of address in the vocative ("my friend"). It is used by the master of the vineyard (20:13), by the king at the wedding (22:12), and by Jesus himself to Judas (26:50). In each case, it expresses a certain equality of status or dignity — even when the situation reveals a rupture or injustice. The context shows that it is a formula of politeness or measured reproach, which recognizes the other as a responsible interlocutor without expressing the intimacy or affection of a deep personal friendship.
G2083.portee: This word reminds us that Jesus addresses even his adversaries with a certain courtesy and dignity. In particular, his use in 26:50 towards Judas shows that Jesus does not deny the established relationship, but names it for what it is in the face of betrayal. For the reader, "friend" invites recognition that every human relationship, even contractual or formal, engages a certain mutual moral responsibility.

sens: Who speaks a foreign, incomprehensible language
G2084.detail: 1. A person or group expressing themselves in a language different from the one known. It is the speech of a foreigner, impossible to understand directly. Paul cites this principle in 1 Corinthians 14:21 to show that the gifts of the Holy Spirit — particularly speaking in tongues — may seem foreign and useless to those who do not understand: like a man speaking an unknown language, the one who speaks in tongues remains misunderstood by his listener.
G2084.origine: The word is composed of two Greek elements: hetero- ("other," "different") and glōssa ("language"). The image is that of the diversity of human languages. This Greek word translates the biblical idea that God can address His people through extraordinary means — including incomprehensible words — to signify His judgment or intervention. In the Old Testament, the expression "men of another tongue" referred to foreign peoples whom God used to speak to Israel.
G2084.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Corinthians 14:21. Paul uses it to illustrate the pastoral problem of the gifts of tongues in the Christian assembly. By quoting Isaiah 28:11-12, he shows that foreign languages — incomprehensible — are a sign addressed to the unbelievers and the rebellious, not an edification for the Church. The context emphasizes the difference between what edifies (the one who prophesies) and what remains obscure (the one who speaks in tongues without interpretation).
G2084.portee: This word reminds us that in the Christian life, spiritual gifts must serve to edify the assembly in understanding. A prophetic or clearly taught word is more valuable than a wonderful gift that remains incomprehensible. It invites everyone to ask themselves: is my service, my word, my life truly useful to those around me, or are they to them a "foreign language"?

sens: Teaching doctrines different from those of Christ and the apostles
Spreading false teaching contrary to sound faith
G2085.detail:
1. The verb literally denotes the action of teaching (didaskaleō) a doctrine "other" or "different" (hetero-) from that which has been received and recognized as true. In 1 Timothy 1:3, Paul charges Timothy to prevent some from doing this in Ephesus: "not to teach other doctrines." 
2. This is not just a variation or nuance, but a false teaching that opposes the "sound words of our Lord Jesus Christ" (1 Timothy 6:3). It is actively propagating a doctrine that Paul qualifies as false, deceptive, which diverts from the authentic apostolic message.
G2085.origine: The word combines hetero- ("other, different") and didaskaleō ("to teach"). This composition suggests the idea of a rupture: not simply teaching, but teaching something foreign or contrary to the received tradition. The pastoral context of the epistles to Timothy shows that this term was forged or at least highlighted to name a very real threat in the churches of the time: the infiltration of false doctrines.
G2085.emploi: The verb appears twice in 1 Timothy, the only two occurrences in the New Testament. In 1:3, Paul orders Timothy to prohibit this teaching in Ephesus. In 6:3, he describes those who "teach false doctrines" as straying from the words of Christ and the doctrine of godliness. In both cases, it is a concrete threat at the time of the early churches: teachers who actively propagate a message deviating from the apostolic deposit. Paul emphasizes the duty of leaders (like Timothy) to oppose it firmly.
G2085.portee: This term reminds the Christian reader that teaching is not neutral: there is a true doctrine (that of Christ and the apostles) and false or distorted doctrines. Local authority (pastors, leaders) must identify and correct those who stray from the received deposit. This invites doctrinal vigilance without naivety: not to receive every teaching that presents itself under the name of "Jesus" or "God," but to measure it against the authentic apostolic word.

sens: to be unevenly yoked, with an ill-matched partner
to be bound to someone in a way that creates imbalance or incompatibility
to form a problematic alliance or partnership with someone who does not share the same faith or values
G2086.detail:
1. The word literally evokes the image of two draft animals yoked together under the same yoke, but in an uneven or unsuitable manner: a strong animal and a weak one, or two different species that cannot work harmoniously. It is a practical problem: the work cannot proceed properly.
2. Figuratively, it denotes an association, commitment, or partnership between two people who are not in the same condition or who do not pursue the same goals. This is the case in marriage or any significant alliance where the two parties have diametrically opposed principles.
3. In 2 Corinthians 6:14, Paul uses this image to forbid believers from forming deep ties (particularly marriage) with unbelievers: righteousness and lawlessness, light and darkness cannot walk together under the same yoke without one of the two being seriously hindered in their faith life.
G2086.origine: The word comes from two Greek elements: "hetero" (other, different) and "zygon" (yoke, bond). It literally denotes the act of being yoked with someone else or something else. The Septuagint, the Greek version of the Old Testament, uses a word from the same family ("heterozygos") to translate the prohibition in Leviticus 19:19: not to plow with an ox and a donkey together, for they do not have the same strength. It is this agricultural image that Paul takes up to speak of unequal marriages and alliances between believers and unbelievers.
G2086.emploi: The verb appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Corinthians 6:14, where Paul addresses the Christians in Corinth who seem to be considering marriages or close partnerships with pagans. The context shows that Paul is not talking about simple social dating, but a bond that would engage a person's entire life (particularly marriage). The apostle uses this agricultural image of the uneven yoke to show that spiritual incompatibility creates a practical and spiritual handicap: two people not moving at the same pace and not sharing the same convictions cannot "plow" together harmoniously.
G2086.portee: For the Christian, this passage reminds us that the choice of marriage or certain significant partnerships is not a purely sentimental or personal matter: it engages our walk with Christ. A union with someone who does not share the same faith creates a permanent tension between radically opposed worldviews. Paul does not say that it is impossible to live together, but that it constitutes an imbalance that affects spiritual and family life. It is a call to wisdom and faithfulness to Christ in the life choices that bind us to others.

sens: Which is distinct; second of a pair
Which differs in nature, quality, or character
Which follows immediately after (the next day, the next time)
The neighbor, the one next to (in terms of social relationship)
Which is not the same, which changes
G2087.detail:
1. This word fundamentally designates what is distinct or second when speaking of two things: "No one can serve two masters. For either he will hate the one and love the other" (Matthew 6:24). It emphasizes the separation between two realities.
2. It also means what differs by its nature or quality — something of a different type: Jesus "appeared in another form" (Mark 16:12), which means a completely distinct aspect.
3. When speaking of time, "other" designates what follows immediately: "the next day" (Acts 20:15), the next time.
4. In social and moral context, it designates the neighbor — one who is not only seen as a neighbor but as someone else, who deserves attention: "in judging others, you condemn yourself" (Romans 2:1).
5. Finally, the word can express change or exchange: when moving from one thing to another, one abandons the first for this one.
G2087.origine: The Greek word ἕτερος comes from a root that properly designates "the second of a pair" (it has a dual origin, common to ancient languages). It primarily translates the Hebrew word אַחֵר (aher) in the Old Testament. It is found in compounds such as ἑτεροδίδασκαλέω (to teach differently) or ἑτερόζυγος (yoked with another, different). The word has gradually come closer to the word ἄλλος (allos, another) in late Greek, with both becoming almost synonymous, although ἕτερος often retains the idea of distinction or pair.
G2087.emploi: This word appears about 95 times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospels of Luke and Matthew, as well as in the Pauline epistles. It is used sometimes to separate two realities ("the one... the other"), and sometimes to introduce another person or thing in a longer series (Acts 2:13: "others mocked"). It designates both what follows chronologically (the next day, Luke 6:6) and what differs by nature (another form, another kind of spiritual gift: 1 Corinthians 12:9-10). Paul uses it to refer to the neighbor to whom we owe love (Romans 13:8) and the one we should not judge (Romans 2:1). Its own nuance remains that of distinction and otherness, rather than simple plurality.
G2087.portee: Understanding this word helps the reader grasp how Jesus and the apostles thought about otherness: not in abstract terms, but as a concrete distinction and often a relationship that cannot be escaped. "You cannot serve two masters" poses a stark choice. And "he who judges others" judges himself, because the other is not distant but your immediate neighbor. This word thus cultivates the idea that our relationship to what is "other" — to God and to men — is central and requires a decision and loyalty.

sens: In a different manner
In a contrary or opposite way
From a different angle or aspect
G2088.detail:
1. In a different manner: the word simply designates a distinct way, another mode of acting or thinking. In Philippians 3:15, Paul says that if the Philippians think differently on certain doctrinal points, God will reveal the truth to them — it is a divergence of understanding or opinion.
2. In a contrary or opposite way: this implies opposition or contradiction, which could threaten unity. But Paul relativizes this divergence by placing his trust in God to gradually correct it.
3. From a different angle: the word can also suggest an alternative perspective or interpretation, without necessarily judging it outright as false, but as incomplete or insufficient until God clarifies it.
G2088.origine: The word comes from the root ἕτερος (heteros, "other, different"), which expresses otherness or distinction between two things. The adverb ἑτέρως is its adverbial form, marking the manner or mode. This root appears in several words of the New Testament: ἑτεροδίδασκαλος (one who teaches another doctrine), ἑτερογενής (of another nature).
G2088.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Philippians 3:15 (according to the best manuscripts). Paul uses it in a pastoral context of exhortation to spiritual unity despite minor doctrinal divergences. These are not serious errors, but points on which believers can still progress in their understanding. This occurrence shows that the New Testament tolerates and manages differences of opinion in the Church, provided that all are moving towards the truth under the guidance of the Holy Spirit.
G2088.portee: This word invites the Christian to distinguish between essential unity (which underpins brotherly communion) and secondary divergences (which can coexist without dividing the Church). For one who fears being wrong or encounters a practice or interpretation different from their own, the text offers a word of wisdom: accept that the path to complete truth is progressive, and that God continues to instruct His people through His Spirit.

sens: Continuity in the present time
Continuity in the past time
Continuity in the future time
Addition, surplus, or complement
Comparison or intensification
Negation: absence, end, or interruption
G2089.detail:
1. The word expresses that something continues now, has not yet ceased. Example: "Paul stayed yet a good while in Corinth" (Acts 18:18), meaning he prolonged his stay there.
2. It marks that something was ongoing at the time of the narrative. Example: "While he was still speaking" (Luke 8:49): Jesus was continuing to speak when the news arrived.
3. It indicates that something will take place in the near future or remains to come. Example: "Once more I will shake not only the earth but also the heaven" (Hebrews 12:26).
4. It signals an addition, a supplement, or what comes to be added. Example: "Call yet two or three witnesses" (Matthew 18:16): additional witnesses are added.
5. It reinforces a comparison or intensification: "your love increases more and more in knowledge" (Philippians 1:9), where "more and more" intensifies the growth.
6. With a negation, it marks the absence or the definitive end. Example: "the salt loses its flavor; how shall it be seasoned? It is good for nothing but to be thrown out" (Matthew 5:13): it can no longer serve any other purpose.
G2089.origine: The Greek word ἔτι comes from an Indo-European root expressing continuation or the passage of time. It is related to other Greek words indicating persistence or duration. It often translates the Hebrew word עוֹד (ʿôd), which literally means "still" or "until" and expresses continuity or addition. This connection with Hebrew shows that the concept of continuation is fundamental in biblical thought.
G2089.emploi: The word ἔτι appears 84 times in the New Testament, primarily in the Gospels (especially Luke and John), and also in the epistles of Paul and the epistle to the Hebrews. It generally expresses continuity in time: either in the present (what lasts now), or in the past (what was still ongoing when an event occurred), or in the future (what will happen in the days to come). It can also indicate an addition, a progression, or a supplement to what already exists. With a negation ("not... yet" or "no... more"), it marks the absence of an action or the final accomplishment of a condition, as in Revelation 20:3 where Satan will no longer be able to deceive the nations. Its usage varies: sometimes it emphasizes the passing of time, sometimes the quantity or intensity that is added.
G2089.portee: This small word helps the reader understand that God acts in history and time. When the Bible says "still," it reminds us that the divine moment is approaching, that nothing is fixed, that waiting has meaning. For the believer, "still" opens hope: what lasts now will end, what is promised will come. It is also a word of patience: it says that things have a time, that change will happen, but not necessarily at the instant.

sens: To arrange, organize the necessary things for an action or event
To make someone ready, to put them in a state to receive or accomplish something
To order, establish in advance (for God or authority)
To prepare a path, a way for someone to pass
To reserve, designate in advance for future use
G2090.detail:
1. To prepare primarily means to materially arrange what is necessary: the disciples "prepared the Passover" by organizing the meal (Matthew 26:19), the women "prepared spices and perfumes" to honor the body of Jesus (Luke 23:56). It is a concrete work of arrangement and organization.

2. To prepare can also mean to make someone internally available or capable: John the Baptist must "prepare a people well disposed for the Lord" (Luke 1:17), meaning to form hearts to receive Jesus. It is to prepare the soul, not just the things.

3. When God prepares, the word expresses His sovereign ordering: He has "prepared" places in heaven for those who love Him (Matthew 20:23), or the kingdom "prepared" before the foundation of the world for the elect (Matthew 25:34). Here, to prepare means to establish, decree, fix in advance.

4. To prepare can also mean to arrange or mark out a way: "Prepare the way of the Lord" (Matthew 3:3) means to level the obstacles, to make it passable for His coming. It is to prepare the passage.

5. Finally, the word can express a capacity suited for a purpose: a vessel "fit for every good work" (2 Timothy 2:21) is a prepared vessel, made ready to serve usefully.
G2090.origine: The word comes from the Greek adjective ἕτοιμος (hetimos) which means "ready," "disposed." Adding the suffix -άζω transforms the adjective into an action verb: "to make ready." In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, this verb often translates כּוּן (kun), which means "to establish," "to strengthen," "to set in place" — the idea of something well-ordered, stable, functional. The family of ἕτοιμος also includes the adverb ἑτοίμως (hetimōs), "willingly," which shows how the word evokes an active availability.
G2090.emploi: The verb appears 40 times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospels and Revelation. It first describes concrete preparations: preparing a meal, spices, lodging, a donkey (Matthew 26:19, Luke 23:56, John 14:2-3). But it also rises in abstraction: preparing a people for the Lord, preparing hearts. Particularly rich is its use in the passive or with a divine subject: God prepares judgment (Matthew 25:41), heavenly places (Matthew 20:23), the world for the saints (1 Corinthians 2:9). Revelation uses it for the marriage of the Lamb and the new Jerusalem (Revelation 19:7; 21:2). The meaning always shifts from the material act to the disposition of the divine will.
G2090.portee: This word reminds Christians that all true preparation engages the body, heart, and spirit. The disciples preparing the Passover meal perform a humble act that anticipates the sacrifice of Jesus — the material order reflects the spiritual order. But above all, meditating on what God has "prepared" — heaven, salvation, judgment — brings us back to humility: our life is not the result of chance, but of a will that precedes us. This invites us to allow ourselves to be prepared: to accept being shaped, disciplined, made fit for service. The word calls for both action and submission.

sens: A readiness and ardent disposition to act
Eagerness to accomplish a task
Preparation of the soul for an action
G2091.detail:
1. The word first designates an inner disposition: the state of one who is ready and enthusiastic, mobilized to act. In Ephesians 6:15, Paul speaks of the "zeal that comes from the Gospel of peace" as a shoe: it is what propels you forward, this impulse of the heart that sets you upright to advance dynamically in the Christian life.
2. It can also express active eagerness to do something, a prepared disposition to obey and serve. It is the opposite of laziness or indifference: a heart that says "yes" even before being asked.
3. Finally, the word evokes a kind of inner foundation: this preparation of the heart that gives stability and assurance to our actions. It comes from the Gospel itself, which firmly establishes us on the rock.
G2091.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb meaning "to prepare" or "to put in order." Its basic image is that of active preparation: to set in place, arrange, dispose of what is necessary. In the Greek translation of the Old Testament, this word often renders Hebrew roots meaning "to establish," "to prepare," "to build solidly." It is a word of action and preparation, not passivity.
G2091.emploi: The word appears only once in Ephesians 6:15, in the famous passage about the armor of the Christian. Paul lists the spiritual protections of God's soldier: the belt of truth, the breastplate of righteousness, the shoes of the Gospel of peace — and he uses this word "zeal" to describe this shoe. The context shows that it is a disposition for battle, a dynamic mobilization to walk forward in faith. It is a weapon, not a weakness.
G2091.portee: For the Christian reading Ephesians 6, this word invites us to understand that spiritual life is not passive or resigned, but active and ardent. This zeal that comes from the Gospel is what makes us advance, allows us to run, to fight the good fight. It is an exhortation to cultivate this inner availability, this preparation of the heart to follow Christ with enthusiasm and eagerness. A Christian without zeal would be like a soldier without shoes: poorly equipped for the road.

sens: Prepared, disposed to be used (for a thing)
Willing, resolved to act or to be acted upon (for a person)
In a state of readiness, without delay
Available, at hand
G2092.detail:
1. For a thing: the feast is ready (Matthew 22:4), the furnished upper room is all ready (Mark 14:15), the time is not ready (John 7:6). The word evokes what has been prepared, completed, set in place and awaits only to be used or consumed.

2. For a person: to be ready means to be disposed, with the intention of doing something. The assassins have committed themselves and are ready to kill Paul (Acts 23:21). The Son of Man will come when you are not ready to receive Him (Matthew 24:44): it is the disposition of the heart, the state of mind.

3. The word often emphasizes imminence, urgency: everything is ready, come now (Luke 14:17). It is what is in working order, without waiting, without delay.

4. In Saint Paul, having something ready or in reserve, like a resource available to act (2 Corinthians 10:6: having ready a punishment for disobedience).
G2092.origine: The Greek word ἕτοιμος comes from a root that evokes arrangement, putting in order. In the Greek Bible of the Old Testament, it mostly translates the Hebrew כּוּן (kun: to establish, to found, to prepare) and מָכוֹן (mâkon: established place, foundation). It is therefore a word that carries the idea of solidity and complete disposition.
G2092.emploi: The word appears 17 times in the New Testament, mainly in Matthew, Luke, and Paul. With things, it describes what is prepared: a feast (Matthew 22:4), a room (Mark 14:15), God's time (John 7:6). With people, it means to be disposed, resolutely oriented towards an action: ready to come to the wedding (Matthew 25:10), ready to die (Luke 22:33), ready to give an answer about one's faith (1 Peter 3:15). Paul also uses it figuratively: having ready a vengeance against disobedience (2 Corinthians 10:6). The word conveys an idea of completeness and immediate availability.
G2092.portee: For the believer, this word invites vigilance: Jesus may return when one is not ready, and true preparation is internal, that of the heart and faith. To be ready to receive the Son of Man or to give an account of one's hope is to live in expectation and faithfulness. It is also to remember that God has prepared what is good for those who fear Him.

sens: Willing to act without hesitation, in complete availability
In a position of readiness or immediate obedience
G2093.detail:
1. The word expresses an active and complete willingness to accomplish something. Paul says in Acts 21:13: "I am ready, not only to be bound but also to die at Jerusalem" — he does not back down; he is fully mobilized for this trial. Similarly, in 2 Corinthians 12:14, "I am ready to come to you" means that he has already resolved to come, without delay or doubt.
2. The word can also describe a capacity or function that is permanently available. In 1 Peter 4:5, it is said that God is "ready to judge the living and the dead" — this means that He is in a constant disposition to render this judgment; He does not defer it; He is always in position for it.
G2093.origine: The word comes from the Greek ἑτοῖμος (hetoimós), which means "prepared, arranged"; the adverb ἑτοίμως conveys the idea of an action or state that proceeds from this preparation. The root evokes an ordering, a prior disposition, like a leveled road or an army lined up to march. It is an active word that speaks less of simple passive availability than of a will that is already crystallized.
G2093.emploi: The word appears only three times in the New Testament. Each time, it is used in a context of personal firmness or divine disposition. In Acts 21:13, it is Paul expressing his resolution to die for Christ. In 2 Corinthians 12:14, it is again Paul announcing his decision to come. In 1 Peter 4:5, it is God Himself who is the subject: the one who is ready to judge. In all cases, the word emphasizes certainty, a fixed will, never a mere possibility.
G2093.portee: This word invites the Christian reader to examine their own disposition. Are we "ready" to follow Christ, as Paul was? It also speaks of the certainty and imminence of divine judgment: God does not hesitate; He does not postpone this judgment; He is perpetually resolved to do so. It is both a call to consecration and a salutary reminder of the seriousness of God's word.

sens: Period of twelve months, annual cycle of time
Duration expressed in number of years
Moment or epoch defined by a year of reign or era
Age of a person measured in years
Length of time in a broad sense, prolonged duration
G2094.detail:
1. The year is primarily the natural measure of time: one revolution of the earth around the sun, or a period of twelve months. This is the simplest and most concrete meaning: "In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar" (Luke 3:1) situates a precise historical moment by counting from the beginning of a king's rule.

2. The word also designates the elapsed interval of time, measured in number of years. When it is said of a woman that she has been afflicted "for twelve years" (Matthew 9:20), it counts the duration of her illness; when it is said "for forty years" (Acts 13:21), it speaks of a period that God has granted.

3. For historical or religious events, the year serves as a dating reference: it is used to fix a moment in time according to an official chronology (the reign of a sovereign, for example).

4. The year also measures the age of people: "over forty years old" (Acts 4:22) means that a person has lived through forty winters and forty summers.

5. More broadly, the word can designate any duration: "Fourteen years later" (Galatians 2:1) simply counts the number of seasons elapsed between two events.
G2094.origine: The Greek word ἔτος (etos) comes from a very ancient root related to the idea of rotation or cycle. In biblical Hebrew, the same reality is designated by שָׁנֶה (shana), which literally means "that which returns," hence "year." The family of the Greek word includes derivatives like ἐνιαυτός (eniautós), more poetic or solemn, which carries the same meaning. The word is simple and universal: it is the common term for measuring time in all ancient languages.
G2094.emploi: The word ἔτος appears 47 times in the Greek New Testament. It is used in the four Gospels to situate events or to measure the duration of an illness or ministry: "for twelve years" (Matthew 9:20), "fifty-six years" of Anna (Luke 2:36). In Acts, it often quantifies durations: "forty years" in the wilderness (Acts 13:20), the age of healed individuals. Paul uses it in his letters to date his own movements: "fourteen years after" his calling in Jerusalem (Galatians 2:1). Revelation counts the thousand years of Christ's reign (Revelation 20:2-7). The word varies little in meaning: it remains the unit of measure of time, whether placed with prepositions ("during," "since," "after") or in the accusative case to answer "how long?"
G2094.portee: The year reminds us that God inscribes the events of salvation in real history, with dates, actors, durations: this is why Luke begins his Gospel with the precise date of Tiberius. Time is not an illusion, but the place where God acts. Counting the years—the year of illness, the year of patience, the year of promise—also teaches us to recognize God's faithfulness through time and the spiritual significance of the seasons of our lives.

sens: In a satisfactory, suitable, correct manner
To perform a good, beneficial action
To be well, to prosper
Exclamation of approval: well done, that's good!
G2095.detail:
1. The word "well" describes a manner of doing that is satisfactory and worthy of approval. It is the opposite of bad: to do something well means to do it correctly, honestly. In Acts 15:29, keeping the stated rules means "doing well," that is, benefiting and finding stability.
2. Doing good means performing a good, generous action that is useful to others. In Mark 14:7, doing good to the poor means helping them concretely, supporting them in need.
3. To be well means to prosper, to live in good health and with success. In Ephesians 6:3, being "well" and living long go together: it is enjoying a good life, free from illness or troubles.
4. It is also an exclamation of encouragement and approval that a master addresses to his servant. In Matthew 25:21 and 25:23, the master says "Well done!" in congratulating his faithful servant, as one would say today "bravo!" or "excellent!"
G2095.origine: The word comes from an ancient root meaning "good, noble, of quality." In Hebrew, this close meaning is found in the verb "tov" (good), which the Greek version of the Old Testament often translates as "eu" when it speaks of doing well or prospering. It is a simple and ancient word, directly linked to the idea of what is worthy, pleasant, and suitable.
G2095.emploi: This small word is infrequent in the New Testament (5 occurrences here), but it carries particular weight each time. In Matthew 25:21-23, it is a word of reward: the master proudly approves the faithful servant. In Mark 14:7, doing good to the poor is a true action, a merciful work. In Acts 15:29, obeying the apostolic decisions means "well" to adhere to this order. In Ephesians 6:3, well-being and longevity are linked to honoring parents: blessing follows obedience. The word changes nuance: moral approval, generous action, prosperity, congratulation.
G2095.portee: This word reminds the reader that God recognizes and rewards faithfulness, even in small things done with care. It is also a call to do good to others without expecting glory, knowing that this pleases God. In reading "well done," the believer hears divine approval and understands that their faithful life is not invisible; it will one day be celebrated like that of the wise servant.

sens: wife of Adam, first woman of humanity
the one who was deceived by the serpent
G2096.detail: 1. Eve is the first woman created by God, companion of Adam and mother of humankind (1 Timothy 2:13 specifies that Adam was formed first, then Eve). 2. She is the one who was deceived by the serpent and ate the forbidden fruit, thus becoming responsible for the entrance of sin into the world: Paul mentions her to warn the Corinthians against any seduction that would lead them away from Christ (2 Corinthians 11:3).
G2096.origine: The name comes from the Hebrew חַוָּה (Havvah), which means "living" or "the one who gives life," related to the root "to live": Eve is named so because she is the mother of all the living (Genesis 3:20). It is the proper name given to the woman whom God took from Adam's rib on the day of creation.
G2096.emploi: Eve is mentioned only twice in the New Testament, both times by Paul. In 1 Timothy 2:13, Paul establishes a creation order: Adam first, Eve second. In 2 Corinthians 11:3, Paul compares Eve's seduction by the serpent to the temptation the Corinthians face of straying from their simple devotion to Christ: the parallel underscores the danger of subtle deception. These two passages place Eve in the history of salvation as a figure of fragility in the face of deception and remind us of the divine order of creation.
G2096.portee: The story of Eve invites the believer to recognize how sin entered the world through seduction and disobedience, and to remain vigilant against the schemes that would divert them from their simple trust in Christ. It also shows that, despite this fall, God has not abandoned humanity, since from her offspring will come the Savior.

sens: To convey a message of joy or salvation
To proclaim the Gospel, the good news of Christ and salvation
To announce liberation in Jesus to the poor and the marginalized
To preach from village to village, from city to city
G2097.detail:
1. The word primarily means to bring a joyful news, a message that delights the listener. It is to announce something good: in Luke 1:19, the angel Gabriel announces to Zechariah the birth of John the Baptist, a joy for an entire nation.
2. In the New Testament, this word mainly refers to the proclamation of the Gospel — the message of salvation in Jesus Christ. Paul says he received this mission to "proclaim" the Gospel to the Gentiles (Galatians 1:16), and the apostles rush to Macedonia to "proclaim the good news" (Acts 16:10).
3. The word carries a social dimension: Jesus says that one of his missions is to "bring good news to the poor" (Luke 4:18), that is, to the small, the forgotten, those whom the world despises.
4. It is a ministry of movement: the disciples "evangelize" from village to village (Luke 9:6, Acts 8:40), planting the seed of the Gospel wherever they go. It is an act of active and itinerant proclamation.
G2097.origine: The word comes from the Greek "eu" (good) and "angelos" (messenger, news). It literally describes one who brings a good message. In the Greek Old Testament, this word translates the Hebrew "bassar," which means "to bring news" — both carry the idea of conveying joyful news. The Old Testament context shows that the "good news" concerns God's blessings and, ultimately, messianic salvation (Isaiah 40:9 and 60:6).
G2097.emploi: This verb appears 52 times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospels and Pauline epistles. In Luke, it describes the central activity of the apostles: Peter and John "proclaim Jesus" (Acts 8:35), Philip "evangelizes" the cities of Samaria (Acts 8:4, 8:25, 8:40), and the disciples go out to "proclaim the good news" from village to village (Luke 9:6). In Paul, the word becomes almost technical: it is his own mission (Romans 1:15, 1 Corinthians 9:16), the heart of his apostleship. Sometimes it is used in the passive — the Gospel "has been proclaimed" (1 Peter 1:25) — or impersonally (1 Peter 4:6). The content varies: peace (Acts 10:36), the Kingdom of God (Luke 8:1), the Resurrection (Acts 13:32), or simply Jesus himself (Acts 8:35).
G2097.portee: This word reveals the passion of God's heart and that of the early Church: the good news of salvation is not to be kept, it is to be shared. For the Christian, it is a call: the Christian faith is by nature missionary — it calls to proclaim everywhere, to both the small and the great, that Jesus saves. It is also an invitation to joy: the one who proclaims the Gospel carries a message of liberation and hope, not of condemnation.

sens: Message of joy announcing a favorable news
Announcement of the kingdom of God and salvation through Christ
The teaching of Jesus and the apostles on salvation
The missionary preaching that brings this announcement
The entirety of the revealed truth concerning Christ and salvation
G2098.detail: 1. The word first designates a happy news, an announcement that brings joy. In ancient Greece, one was even rewarded for bringing good news. 2. In the New Testament, "good news" takes on a precise meaning: it is the announcement that the kingdom of God has come and that salvation is offered through Christ (Mark 1:15). Jesus himself preaches this good news of the kingdom in the synagogues of Galilee (Matthew 4:23). 3. The word also refers to the fundamental teaching of the apostles: the message of grace and salvation that they received from the Lord Jesus and that they proclaim (Acts 20:24). Paul speaks of "his" good news, the one he received by revelation. 4. By extension, it is the very act of preaching, of announcing this teaching: "This good news of the kingdom will be proclaimed throughout the world" (Matthew 24:14). 5. It is also the truth of salvation in Christ, which can be referred to as "truth" or "hope" (Galatians 2:5; Colossians 1:23). The same "good news" can be presented from different angles: that of Christ, that of the Father, that of grace, that of the glory of the blessed God.
G2098.origine: The Greek word comes from two roots: "eu" (good) and "aggelia" (message, news). The Hebrew "bsora" (בְּשׂוֹרָה), which literally means "good news," regularly renders it. The word evokes the image of a messenger running to bring happy news. In the Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Old Testament), it also translates passages where a prophet announces a favorable event from God.
G2098.emploi: The word appears 72 times in the New Testament. The Gospels use it to describe the preaching of Jesus: he "preaches the good news of the kingdom" (Matthew 4:23, 9:35). Mark opens his Gospel with "Jesus preached the good news of God" (Mark 1:14-15). Acts shows Peter and the apostles preaching this good news in Jerusalem and beyond (Acts 15:7). Paul, more than anyone else, speaks of the "good news": it is for him the heart of his apostolic ministry. He sometimes calls it "his" good news (Romans 2:16, 16:25), sometimes the good news of Christ, of the Father, or of the glory of God, depending on the aspect he emphasizes. In his letters, the good news is inseparable from the notion of truth, hope, and faith. It does not primarily designate a text or a book, but the living message of salvation in Christ.
G2098.portee: The "good news" is not primarily a doctrine among others: it is the news of salvation offered in Christ, to which one responds by repentance and faith (Mark 1:15). It highlights that the Christian message brings not condemnation, but joy. Understanding what the good news is invites every Christian to truly believe in it and to conform their life to it, but also to carry it to others. It is Good News primarily because it brings true hope: the kingdom of God is near, and God offers grace through Christ.

sens: one who announces the good news of Jesus Christ
one who has received the special gift of preaching the Gospel with power
author of a Gospel account
G2099.detail:
1. An evangelist is primarily someone who announces the good news of Christ — the Gospel. He is a preacher who carries the message of salvation in Jesus everywhere. Philip, referred to as "the evangelist" in Caesarea (Acts 21:8), had this primary mission: to proclaim the Gospel.

2. In the New Testament Church, the evangelist is recognized as a specific function or gift, distinct from apostles, prophets, pastors, and teachers (Ephesians 4:11). It is a special ability given by the Spirit to effectively announce the Word and convert souls to Christ.

3. The evangelist does not merely believe and follow as a disciple: he is active in ministry. Timothy is urged to "do the work of an evangelist" (2 Timothy 4:5), meaning to dedicate his energy to this urgent proclamation of the Gospel.
G2099.origine: The Greek word comes from "eu-angelia": "eu" (good) and "angelia" (message, announcement). An evangelist is literally "one who brings good news." It is the same root that gives us "Gospel" in French. The suffix "-istès" designates one who performs a function or possesses a quality, much like an artisan practices his craft.
G2099.emploi: The word appears three times in the New Testament. It first designates a recognized function in the early Church: a gift from the risen Christ to the body of believers (Ephesians 4:11), on par with apostles or pastors. Philip embodies this role (Acts 21:8): he is known for his proclamation activity. The phrase "do the work of an evangelist" (2 Timothy 4:5) shows that this ministry is active, requiring commitment and perseverance. The usage remains consistent: it is always one who announces the Gospel.
G2099.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that the announcement of the Gospel is not reserved for apostles: it is a living ministry in the Church. It also shows that the ordinary Christian can be called to fulfill this work according to his gifts. It is an invitation to take seriously the proclamation of Christ as a responsibility and a blessing: not an isolated task, but a valid and useful role for the entire body.
